speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Monteith (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: TABLING OP REPORT ON PROCEDURES RESPECTING NEW DRUGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have now received the report of the special committee on new drugs appointed at my request by the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada to examine the present departmental procedures for dealing with new drugs, the requirements of the regulations under the Food and Drugs Act, and any other matters felt to be relevant to the issue. With the permission of the house I should like to table this report and offer a few introductory comments on it.
At the outset I should like to express my deepest thanks to the royal college for having established such an effective and hard working committee. Possibly the best way to express my thanks to the committee is to say that I find myself in complete agreement with the conclusions it has drawn and the recommendations it has made, and I am anxious to move forward as quickly as possible to achieve the objectives described in the report.
As the house will see, this document should prove to be of great value in the government's current study to find the best means of ensuring that the Canadian public continues to receive the utmost protection in this age of scientific and medical advancement. Under the chairmanship of Dr. F. S. Brien the committee has gone into the subject in a wealth of detail, receiving a considerable number of submissions from Canadian sources and much assistance from U.S. authorities. Dr. Brien, and his associates Dr. Dufresne and
Dr. Sellers, must be congratulated on the manner in which they have come to the heart of the problem, and on the forthright way in which they suggest the steps that should now be taken.
The committee has clearly stated that the underlying purpose of the Food and Drugs Act is not the impossible objective of eliminating risks associated with the use of drugs, but the more practical one of keeping such risks to a minimum. It also recognizes that it would be quite impractical to suggest that all drug testing be assigned to a government agency. Its principal recommendations involve increases in the directorate's professional staff and the provision of further discretionary powers to the minister, permitting the immediate withdrawal of a drug from sale or other changes in its status when it is felt that the need for such action has arisen.
We have already made certain moves toward remedying the staff situation and are making progress in other respects. I would hope that the special committee of the house on food and drugs will turn its attention to this report, and I shall be pleased to go into further detail at that time.
With its formal report the royal college committee sent to me a considerable number of appendices containing documents and reports it had referred to in the course of its deliberations. In view of the bulk of this material it has not yet been possible to take copies from the originals, and with the permission of the house I should like to table copies of the report now and undertake to deposit copies of the appendices with the Clerk as soon as these are available.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this afternoon I intend to go over the broad outlines of various questions in the sphere of internationl affairs in which Canada is directly interested. As hon. members will realize, it will not be possible to go into great detail on any of these particular subjects.
3086	HOUSE OF
Supply-External Affairs
Before I proceed with that review, may I express the belief that we have now moved into a new era in the world, largely because of certain developments which have taken place within the last few months or which will take place within the next few months, each one of which has very far reaching implications. For example, there is the movement of Great Britain into the European community. We all know it is not yet certain whether that move will be made; but no matter whether it is or is not, what has happened in connection with that proposal as between Great Britain and the six countries of continental Europe is bound to have very far reaching effects. In the last day or two we have seen France and West Germany signing a treaty of friendship covering political questions, economic questions and defence questions. There is a great shifting going on in Europe, and no one can tell at this time what the end result will be.
That brings up another far reaching development. I believe that in the commonwealth at the present time we are in a state of flux. I had the privilege of attending the prime ministers' conference in September of last year, and naturally every one of the delegates there was very much interested in the question whether Great Britain would go into the European community, and what the future of the commonwealth was to be. Whether one thought that Great Britain should or should not go in, a great deal of thought was given to the future of the commonwealth. I think the value of the commonwealth was impressed upon the mind of everyone there, and I have no doubt on the minds of millions of people in the various nations of the commonwealth.
Again in the field of trade, we are now in a period when very far reaching changes may take place in the trade carried on in various parts of the world. That question, of course, was of great importance in connection with the British and European community negotiations, but it is also important in many other spheres. I recall to hon. members at this point the statement which was made by our own Prime Minister at the prime ministers' conference with regard to this question, when he made a proposal which I think can roughly be described from the following notes of his comments:
I propose that this conference should declare its intention to extend an invitation to all member nations of the commonwealth, of the E.E.C., E.F.T.A., the U.S.A. and Japan and other like minded nations, indicating a desire to participate, to meet at the earliest practicable date to give consideration as to how to deal with the trading problems before us in a way which will be to the mutual advantage of all.
That idea or something very much like it may very well be the course that is followed


eventually. However, hon. members will recall that in the next month, in October of last year, the United States congress approved important new trade legislation under which the United States was to participate in forthcoming international tariff negotiations. At that time, in an exchange of letters between our Prime Minister and President Kennedy, it was agreed that Canada and the United States should take the initiative in proposing a meeting of the ministers of the GATT contracting parties to discuss important trade developments and to make plans for the GATT tariffs and trade conference. That has now been carried out. A joint Canada-United States proposal for such a ministerial meeting was accepted in November of 1962 and the GATT council, which is not, of course, a ministerial council, is to meet on February 18. It will set a date for this ministerial meeting, and it is expected that the ministerial meeting of GATT will be held about the middle of May.
Then at about roughly the same time in the United Nations the underdeveloped countries were pressing for a United Nations world conference. There was a good deal of discussion about that in the second committee, and finally it was decided that there would be a United Nations world trade conference, which will be concerned primarily with the broad range of trade and development problems of the less developed countries; and this conference is to be held early in 1964. Canada, by the way, took a very prominent part in bringing about agreement on the terms of that resolution in the United Nations. There was a dispute between the less developed countries and the large trading countries as to the time at which the conference was to be held, but we were able to bring about a settlement of that difficulty. All these movements are going on, or are about to go on, in the field of trade. I suggest that this will be an extremely significant trade year for all parts of the world, and particularly for Canada, because we are as vitally interested in world trade as any other country.
Another development of far reaching implication has been the successful settlement by President de Gaulle of the trouble in Algeria. This had the whole Arab world in a turmoil and was causing trouble with all the African countries. It was a great bleeding wound for France herself, and was a problem which appeared almost impossible of solution. Yet that problem is at least well on the way to settlement, and I think the fact there has been such a settlement will be of great importance in the months ahead.
Then, of course, there was the Cuban episode. There the Americans, acting with

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
firmness and I think with moderation-I suggest with moderation-achieved great success. The Cuban episode has made perfectly clear that in the world today the preponderance of power is with the United States. No longer is it a question of two great equal nuclear powers. I suggest that at the present time the United States is beyond any shadow of doubt preponderant in power. That, Mr. Chairman, may constitute quite a temptation. When you are the biggest fellow in the school yard it is quite a temptation to shove everybody else around. Now, I am confident that there will be no such development in United States policy. I am confident that they will not adopt a policy of getting tough with their allies. For Canada, of course, it is particularly important whether anything of that kind develops.
Another outstanding development has been the success of the United Nations in the Congo within the last few days. That was the most difficult operation this great world organization had ever undertaken. I have no doubt that every member in this chamber has wondered many times how on earth the United Nations would ever get out of the Congo and also how they would ever be able to bring about any order in that unhappy country. Yet they are well on the way now. The premier of Katanga met the United Nations troops when they drove into Kolwezi and welcomed them there, and took the stand that his state would be part of the nation of the Congo. This means a great deal in building up the prestige of the United Nations and a great deal in bringing about world order.
The United Nations also had another big lift or a great impetus from the fact that in the Cuban crisis the United States and the Soviet union rushed right into the U.N. in an effort to get some agreement worked out. They did not stand outside. They did not just ignore the United Nations and go about working things out themselves or anything like that. They went to the United Nations and Secretary General U Thant did a statesmanlike job in helping to work out an agreement on Cuba.
Another development which I think is very far reaching has been the steady reduction in the number of colonies. This colonialism question has been a difficult and nasty one in the United Nations and all over the world. Most of the former dependent countries now have their independence. There are a few more to come, and I am confident that they will gain independence in due course. However, quite a large segment of that problem has been settled. There is one which remains to be dealt with and in which our own nation of Canada took the lead, namely the question of Soviet imperialism or what happens inside
Supply-External Affairs the present Soviet union. These Soviet representatives have been very quick and very bold about attacking Great Britain, and France in the United Nations for what they have been doing about colonies. However, there has not been in the Soviet union one little move to give the people within their boundaries any right at all to decide whether or not they wish to have their independence back again. Hence this issue is one which will still have to be dealt with.
Another far reaching development has been the attack by red China on India. That was an amazing action which it is hard for any Canadian to understand. Here was India, one of the leaders of the unaligned countries, which was certainly giving no offence to the red Chinese and doing nothing to justify aggression of that kind, yet red China struck. It does not require much imagination to realize that this action will have a far reaching effect in all the unaligned countries. I am confident that they are watching that action and that they will have made some decisions which certainly will not be against the interests of western nations such as Canada.
Then there has been the disagreement between the Soviet union and red China. For many months now we have heard rumours about arguments going on in the communist camp. I do not think it is ever wise to put too much credence in reports of that type, for should anything develop leading to really serious trouble I have no doubt they would get together again very quickly. However, the argument has gone on, it has grown louder and it has come out into the open, until when they were meeting in East Germany last week they were observed to be really going at it just in the way we sometimes go at each other in the House of Commons. Wonders will never cease. As I say, this development may have very far reaching effects.
Then another development with far reaching implications has been the recognition by every leader in every nation of the world of impending doom-and I repeat the words "of impending doom"-if there is a nuclear war or if no method of living together can be devised. Across this world today there is a will for peace such as there never has been previously. One needed only to go to the United Nations at the last session and be there while the Cuban crisis was under way in order to realize that mankind, as represented there by the delegates from 110 countries, was determined that something had to be done, and quickly, in order to bring about world peace for hundreds of millions of people who otherwise would perish from this earth.
As I see it, these are the main developments which have taken place or are in the process

Supply-External Affairs of taking place and which have much wider implications than has been the case at any other time since I have had the privilege of being Secretary of State for External Affairs.
The question may be asked, where does Canada fit into this picture? May I say that Canada is involved and is helping in an idealistic way all over the world. I mention first the field of disarmament. I deal with that first because this is the main way in which world peace can eventually be achieved. This is where effort is most worth while.
By disarmament I do not mean simply stopping the development of more deadly weapons or reducing existing weapons, although such results would be of the utmost importance; I define it in the wider sense as including the stopping of nuclear weapons tests, stopping the pollution of the air that we, our children and our grandchildren will have to breathe, reducing tensions, reducing distrust. It is very hard to bring about any settlement as long as nations distrust each other so that every word one says the other disbelieves instantaneously. I include all activities of that kind under disarmament.
Canada is involved in this question for good reason. We just happen to lie between the two great nuclear powers. If there is a nuclear war we are in for it. Our cities will be destroyed. On the Saturday night after the Cuban crisis arose I believed, and I have no doubt many other people did, that before morning Ottawa might be demolished, as well as Montreal, Toronto and my home city of Vancouver. Canada has another good reason to be interested in questions having to do with disarmament, for we are in a heavy fallout area. This nation is in one of the worst fall-out areas in the world, the temperate zone. It is admitted that Canada is in one of the worst areas. Fall-out may affect not only us but the very food we grow, and no one knows yet what the end result will be of the nuclear tests which have already taken place, because a lot of the fall-out is not yet down. Questions were asked just today about strontium 90 in the food Eskimos in northern Canada are eating.
The government believes that Canada can do something worth while on the question of disarmament. One reason is because we were chosen by our western colleagues in NATO as one of the NATO negotiators on the ten-nation committee set up in September of 1959, and I would point out that this does not look as though we were quite as low in the esteem of NATO as some of our friends opposite would have the Canadian people believe. Five NATO countries, Great Britain,

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
the United States, France, Italy and Canada, and five communist countries, the Soviet union, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Bulgaria and Rumania, formed the committee.
Then there is the question of our position vis-a-vis Great Britain and the United States. Our relationships with these two countries are such that we can talk to them on this or any other issue on a more intimate basis than any other country in the world. Another reason we believe that Canada can do something worth while is that we happen to have the confidence of practically all the unaligned countries in the world. I do not believe there is a country of the NATO group or of the Warsaw pact group that has nearly as many friends among the unaligned countries as Canada has, and that is because these nations have confidence in us.
Another reason we believe that Canada can do something on this question is that we have as our chief disarmament negotiator Lieutenant General E. L. M. Burns, a distinguished Canadian with a splendid record in both wars, a record as head of the United Nations emergency force, a splendid record in the civil service, a man who in my judgment is the best qualified man in the world today on the question of disarmament. He certainly has the respect of the delegates of every one of the 16 nations participating in the present disarmament negotiations, including the communist countries.
The ten-nation committee was set up in September of 1959 by the four western foreign ministers, not by the United Nations. The committee tried to work out some agreement but on June 27, 1960, all the communist delegates got up and walked out. The chairman at the time happened to be from one of the communist countries and he refused to hear any western delegates. He heard the delegates from the other four communist countries; then the delegates from the five countries picked up their brief cases and out they went. That was not a very promising development from the point of view of anyone interested in the field of disarmament.
However, the Americans worked with us on this issue in a spirit of splendid co-operation and we managed to get a meeting of the United Nations disarmament commission. The communists said they were not going to attend and were going to boycott the meeting, and they boycotted it right up to the time we were about to meet in New York. But when India and all the other unaligned countries made it perfectly clear that they were going to be there anyway, in came the communist delegates at the last minute, and we had a pretty good meeting of the United

Nations disarmament commission. This was not a meeting of the United Nations, although the nations were the same, but a meeting of the commission and, by the way, it has not met since.
A resolution was approved unanimously urging the resumption of disarmament negotiations at once. The Russians voted for it too. But then nothing happened. However, it was an expression of world opinion. At the meeting of this commission we demanded that negotiations be resumed, and we urged that representatives of the unaligned countries be added to the negotiators. There was no use sending back the five Warsaw pact countries and the five NATO countries, because they would clash in the first 15 minutes and that would be it. So Canada urged that representatives of the unaligned countries be added.
The general assembly of the United Nations met a few weeks after that, in the fall of
1960.	At that time the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) was my parliamentary secretary and he took a magnificent part in the deliberations at the United Nations. He really carried the ball for Canada. We stressed the need to resume negotiations from the start to the finish of that session. We insisted that the disarmament negotiations had to be resumed. I remember he telephoned me once at Goose Bay where I had just landed for half an hour in returning from Europe. He happened to get me and he said, "Things are getting pretty tough down here. I am afraid we are going to get a good licking if we go ahead and force a vote on this particular resolution." We talked for a few minutes and then we decided we would go ahead and force a vote anyway. We took a good licking just to show that we meant business on this question of resuming the disarmament negotiations.
At the same time, starting really in 1959, we had been bringing in resolutions about radiation with the idea of focusing world opinion on the menace of these nuclear weapons tests. We have been getting these resolutions carried with more support every year. This year we did not have nearly as much trouble, I will tell you, as we did in 1959. In 1961 the Soviet union, if you please, resumed tests. They had been negotiating the question with the United States and Britain for nearly three years. During all that time there had been a voluntary moratorium. Then in September, 1961, out they come and start tests. Obviously they had been making preparations for several months.
When the United States general assembly met in 1961 the Soviet union was in the middle of these tests. Perhaps you will recall that they were going to set off a 100 megaton bomb
Supply-External Affairs and Canada and the Scandinavian countries- Canada nearly always works with them in the United Nations-took the lead in bringing in a resolution urging Premier Khrushchev not to set off that bomb. There again we had a lot of trouble, because some nations said what is the use? In the meantime he set off a bomb, and everybody thought it was a 100 megaton bomb. Then, fortunately, we discovered it was only 50 megatons, so our resolution still made sense the way it was worded against the 100 megaton bomb. In the final analysis, that resolution carried with the support of all the nations except the communist countries.
By this time opinion had been aroused about this testing, and in December of 1961 the United States and Russia reached agreement that there would be an 18-nation disarmament committee, and they named the committee.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am very grateful to hon. members for allowing me to continue. Agreement was reached by all the members of the United Nations to set up this 18-nation disarmament committee including the same five countries from the west and the same five from the east, plus eight unaligned countries as we had been urging. Those countries were India, Burma, Sweden, United Arab Republic, Ethiopia, Nigeria, Brazil and Mexico. They met at Geneva in March of last year. Mind you, only 17 countries met, because for some reason or other France declined to participate. The western countries are now only four, namely, Great Britain, the United States, Italy and Canada.
At the meeting in Geneva we took the lead in urging that the United States and the Soviet union be joint chairmen of that committee. This had worked very well in the conference on Laos, and we thought it would help to have them as co-chairmen of the disarmament committee. This was agreed to. I feel it is a good idea because, in reality, if these two countries do not reach agreement there is not going to be any agreement, and it is wise to have the responsibility directly on them. It has some disadvantages. I think that having nuclear weapons, they do not have the same sense of urgency about getting some agreement worked out that the rest of us do. I know the disarmament committee was to meet on January 15, of this year, but these two nations got together and decided it should
3070	HOUSE OF
Supply-External Affairs not meet until February 12. However, in the meantime they are carrying on what could be very useful. By the way, we did not agree to the delay. We thought it was a mistake to postpone the meeting.
In the disarmament committee negotiations the eight unaligned countries have played an excellent part. I never hesitate to pay tribute to them for their objectivity and for their sincerity, for the way in which they are trying to help bring about agreement. There is a subcommittee on nuclear test ban problems. We tried to have that subcommittee comprised of the three nuclear powers plus some of the others, but they would not agree. There are only three nations on that subcommittee.
Then there is a committee of the whole on collateral measures. This was a Canadian idea. We thought there were some issues which did not come directly within the terms of the disarmament treaty which could be dealt with collaterally and dealt with quickly, that if agreement could be reached on some of these collateral measures, it might help open the door for agreement of a more extensive kind. The first collateral measure considered was war propaganda, a declaration against any of the countries using war propaganda. Agreement was reached on that in the committee of the whole. The Russians agreed to that. They had much to say about changing the words, putting in "these" and "its" and so on, but agreement was finally reached.
Just the day before the agreement was to be approved in plenary session, word came from Moscow that there had to be four or five additional conditions attached to it, all of which were obviously cold war conditions and which made agreement impossible. It was a very good example of Moscow pulling the rug out from underneath their own negotiator. The person involved here was Mr. Zorin, who had the rug pulled out from under him just a few weeks ago in New York.
In so far as this question of collateral measures is concerned, there are three which are in line for consideration. One is a measure to prohibit the launching of weapons of mass destruction from outer space. This was a Canadian idea. Last March, nearly a year ago, when this collateral measures committee was first set up, we walked in with a declaration to the effect that weapons of mass destruction were not to be used in outer space, that they could not be launched from outer space. Well, that threw everybody into a tizzy. I mean there was a good deal of discussion, and it was not accepted with any degree of enthusiasm by some of the bigger countries. The Russians finally said "We do not want to talk about that; we will leave that for negotiation in connection with the treaty." In any event,


this is one question we hope will be considered by this collateral measures committee.
Another suggestion was a measure to reduce the risk of war by accident, miscalculation or failure of communication. Proposals have been made to reduce the risk of accidental war through improved communication between governments, advance notification of military manoeuvres, the establishment of observation posts and the exchange of military missions between east and west.
Another subject which is to be considered in that committee is measures to prevent the wider dissemination of nuclear weapons. In the main negotiations on a disarmament treaty the Americans have put in a draft treaty and so have the Russians, and a lot of time has been spent trying to piece them together. Canada has aimed at picking out points where there was almost agreement and in stressing those points, trying to bring about agreement on those things in the belief that once the two sides agreed on a paragraph of that kind, it would be easier to go on and agree on something a little more difficult.
We went back to the general assembly last fall, and one thing that everyone was agreed on in New York was that the disarmament committee should carry on its work negotiating a treaty. There was no difference of opinion about that.
There was trouble about nuclear test banning. The Soviet side wanted one resolution; the Americans wanted another resolution. In fact there was a lot of difficulty in working out a resolution dealing with the question of a nuclear test ban. Canada moved in on that, and in my judgment this was our main accomplishment in the last session. We were able to bring about agreement on a resolution on the question of negotiating for a nuclear test ban. We based our offensive on the letters which had been exchanged between President Kennedy and Premier Khrushchev at the time of the Cuban crisis. They each wrote saying "We must now get together and settle the rest of the problems. Why could we not do this about a test ban?" We picked that up, and with the impetus of those letters behind us we were able to help bring about a resolution which became known as the Canadian resolution, although we had only submitted amendments, and this resolution was endorsed by everybody except the communists, who abstained.
The disarmament committee resumed on November 26 and worked until December 20, when it adjourned until January 15 and, as I explained a few minutes earlier, that date has been put back until February 12. In the meantime developments have taken place which may be, and I hope will be, of great

significance. There has been this exchange of letters between President Kennedy and Premier Khrushchev which were printed as an appendix to Hansard some two days ago, and the Americans, the Russians and the British are now meeting in Washington trying to bring about an agreement on the terms of a test ban. They have made considerable progress. The main difference between them at the moment is as to the number of automatic seismic stations which there will be in Russia and on the number of times an international team can be sent in to inspect those stations. The Russians have agreed to three inspections annually, although until a few days ago they were saying they would not agree to any inspections of any kind; the Americans have asked for eight to ten inspections.
It is of the utmost importance that agreement be reached on this question. If they could reach agreement on a test ban then it would stop radiation, and would lead to the possibility of making settlements on other disarmament problems. In any event, Canada will continue her efforts to bring about a reasonable settlement, and I think today Canada is generally recognized as the leader in the field of working out some disarmament agreement between the east and the west.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
So much for Canada's activities in the field of disarmament. Then there is a related activity, and that is the field of peace keeping. Mind you, Mr. Speaker, if we are able to bring about a measure of disarmament there will be more and more peace keeping work to be done. The two go together, and in my judgment peace keeping in the world under U.N. auspices is going to become steadily more important. Canada is ideally situated for this role and, with India, Canada is today the most experienced nation in the world in the peace keeping field.
Take, for example, the Congo. We have been in the Congo from the start. The house authorized the sending of up to 500 personnel, and Canada has been running the communications system for the United Nations in the Congo, taking a very active part in the air services, and also in the staff work for the whole United Nations force. A lot of this work is done by bilingual Canadians, French speaking Canadians, and all over the world there is a job now to be done by Canadians who are French speaking. In the Congo they are the leaders in Canadian activities.
Canada is also represented on the secretary general's Congo advisory committee at the United Nations. There are only three western
Supply-External Affairs countries on it, Sweden, Ireland and Canada, with 17 African and Asian countries. We are able to consult with the secretary general on Congo questions at any time, and are able to advise him and the other members of that committee. I think those members of the house who have been at the United Nations will agree that Canada's actions in connection with the Congo have been of great benefit. We have tried to keep tempers cool. We have tried to urge moderation, and I think we have been able to do quite a lot in that regard.
Our policy in regard to the Congo has been throughout, and is today, to support the United Nations. Some of the western countries have not taken that stand. The French have been against the Congo operation and pay nothing toward its expenses. The British have been very worried about it and have not been as energetic in support of the United Nations as Canada has been. But I repeat that our policy is to support the United Nations in the Congo.
We have also taken action to help in the financing of the Congo operation. Providing the money has been a tremendous problem. It is costing about $10 million a month for that operation, and the United Nations has almost gone bankrupt paying for it. In passing I may say I thought the Globe and Mail of January 23, 1963 summed up our accomplishments in the Congo very well when it said in an editorial headed "The U.N. and International Co-operation":
Many nations took a constructive part, and will continue to do so, in the Congo operation, but perhaps special mention should be given to India. Nigeria, Malaya, Ethiopia, Ireland, Sweden, Tunisia -and Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on a question of privilege, I was here until half past three, for the first half hour the minister spoke. At that time-as he would tell you if his voice were good enough at the moment-I went to meet the ambassador for Korea on an appointment that had been made some considerable time ago. Hon. members will perhaps recall that the ambassador for Korea saw the Governor General yesterday and presented his credentials. I have just come down from seeing the ambassador for Korea, and that is the reason I was absent for some 20 minutes.

Mr. Chairman, one would have thought that a matter of this importance, in this new era which the minister has mentioned, would be one in which the defence policy would run consistently with foreign policy. It is inconceivable that our foreign policy would be determined by the character and nature of defence policy. Clearly foreign policy must determine not only defence but international commercial policy. At a time when defence does play such an important part in our national considerations I offer no excuse for the statement I make, which involves a sincere and strong belief on my part that

there must be the closest consistency between the formulation and declaration of foreign policy and the implementation of defence policy.
Mr. Chairman, in his statement the minister gave us, as is his practice-and about this I make no complaint-a tour d'horizon of the situation in the world as he sees it since he last spoke to us. It will be recalled that that was some time ago. This is the first time since this parliament was convened that we have had any statement from the Secretary of State for External Affairs which could be characterized as a general survey of Canada's foreign policy.
In his statement today the minister reviewed some of the important events of the past year. He reviewed the settlement in Algeria. He mentioned the Chinese aggression against India; and I may say, by way of parenthesis, that what he said in this connection will be widely supported in this house and in this country. Our sympathies are with this commonwealth country, India, with whom we have had, and I am sure will continue to have, the closest and understandable ties. All the assistance that we can give to India, together with other countries such as the United Kingdom and the United States, will be given. Any policy in this regard put forward by the government of Canada will receive the widest measure of support in this house.
The minister said we were entering a new era. I hope he will not misunderstand me if I say that if this is the case, there has been nothing in his statement thus far which indicates any orientation in the foreign policy of our country that seemingly takes into account the opening of this new era. What the minister said was important. His report about disarmament, the nuclear test talks, the resurgence of the strength of the United Nations, these are important events; but they do not represent in themselves any developments which could be regarded as outside the character and the context of the kind of problems of the so-called other era which we have dealt with from time to time in this house. It is true that developments in the world today do cause great concern. There have been some developments which warrant a conviction that in the year 1962 some progress was made in international affairs on a world scale. We have seen, as the minister pointed out, increasing evidence of a fragmentation in the communist bloc, with a seemingly ever widening gulf between Moscow and Peking. Of course, we must make sure that this widening gulf does not

cause us to be overly optimistic or ill prepared for contrary eventualities which might well ensue in the relation between these two important powers.
We have been through the crisis over Cuba, serving clearly to emphasize how completely interdependent the free world has become and how much we rely on the concept of the deterrent possessed by the United States. We came through the Cuban crisis, Mr. Chairman, as a result of this deterrent and the strong, forceful and courageous diplomacy of the President of the United States.
This matter is one of such importance that we have the duty to ask ourselves what is the position which our country took in respect of a matter that not only involved the peace of the world but the preservation of the North American communities, including Canada. While there was displayed by the chief executive in the United States the kind of firmness which in the situation was necessary, I do not believe the same can be said for the government of Canada in that same situation. The government properly has insisted upon fullness of consultation between the various members of the western alliance. This is an insistence which all of us in this house will support. No nation can remain free and no alliance of free nations can remain a free alliance if this principle is not in all practical and possible situations observed.
I suggest that the record of the week of the Cuban crisis will demonstrate that there was justification for concern on the part of the people of Canada over the direction given to this country by the government in that critical situation. I well remember questions being put to the ministry by members of the opposition groups with regard to the Cuban crisis. The Prime Minister cautioned us as to the desirability of there being a minimum of interrogation and that there be no question put which did not bear the stamp of full responsibility. With that characterization I do not quarrel. But I remember that that same evening the foreign minister of this country went on the television and was interrogated by newspapermen, who put questions to him not unlike some of the questions which had been put by hon. members of this house to members of the government. I must say to my hon. friend the Secretary of State for External Affairs that the positions which he took that night over the television-not in this house- were such as to contribute considerably to the lack of confidence which the people of Canada had at that time in the conduct of the foreign policy of the government.
Mr. Chairman, it seems to me the Cuban crisis highlighted once again the need for Canada to take part in the organization of
Supply-External Affairs American states. This was emphasized well over a year and a half ago by the visit of the secretary of state for external affairs to several Latin American countries and by the visit of the Prime Minister to Mexico. Since that time, during which there was a further suggestion made in this very chamber by the President of the United States, we have had from the government no indication as to what is the policy of the government or its view in that regard. This matter is not unrelated to the Cuban crisis. It will be recalled that it was a salutary experience to have ministers of the council of the organization of American states meeting on the eve of the greatest crisis since the second world war to discuss the possibility, indeed that evening the likelihood, of nuclear weapons being fired upon North America, and Canada not even being present at the meeting. Of course, Canada had no right to go there as a member, but I well recall the suggestion made by the Leader of the Opposition, that perhaps some way could be found by which Canada as an interested party-and this cannot be denied- might have had an opportunity of sitting at the table. In the light of events currently in Cuba, in the light of events in other Latin America countries, involving as they do fundamental economic readjustments which will have their implications in the relations which will prevail between that particular area and the rest of the world, it seems to me that the time was never more urgent for us to accept the long-standing invitation of every member of the organization of American states and to join this organization.
Mr. Chairman, these are vital matters, and as the minister said events which are now unfolding indicate that we have to be ever vigilant if we want to make sure that we are not the object of destruction. It is an elementary principle in government that the government of the day should regard as its first obligation, the taking of every possible step to make sure that it has so arranged its procedures in national life to guarantee the preservation and the integrity of the nation. This is the standard by which we will judge, and by which in duty we must judge, the conduct of this government in the days that lie ahead and in respect of the events of the immediate past.
I agree with the Secretary of State for External Affairs that the Cuban crisis has shown that the United Nations has not lost its force and its value. Indeed, the Cuban crisis demonstrated the importance of the United Nations. However, we should remember that it is illusory to think that the United Nations can impose solutions upon great powers like the United States or the Soviet union. But the United Nations can by its good

Supply-External Affairs offices, as was demonstrated in the case of Cuba, provide the channel for a change of policy by a great power. It is not without significance that the United States, after what were thought to be necessary precautions were taken, did go to the United Nations. But what the United Nations can do is to supervise and inspect a solution, and that it has done in Cuba and in other situations.
Speaking about the United Nations, I am sure that my hon. friend will agree that 12 months ago it looked as though the cold war might destroy or seriously impair the usefulness of this collective security organization. We know that the death of the former secretary general was used by the Soviet union to press for a troika secretary generalship which would have reduced the United Nations to impotence. At the end of last year the unanimous decision to establish in that important office U Thant gave the United Nations a new hope and a new opportunity; and it is not without significance, as the Leader of the Opposition has pointed out elsewhere, that the three executive chairs at the United Nations general assembly are now filled by gentlemen who come from Asia.
I note with satisfaction, as has the minister himself, that the near settlement-what we hope will be the final settlement-of the Congo problem represents a major achievement of the United Nations, and particularly in the final days, to the determination and persistence of the United States.
Mr. Chairman, the minister referred in his speech to the important developments now taking place in Europe in regard to Britain's application for participation in the European common market. Recent weeks have shown a deterioration, however, in our hopes for Britain's taking this historic step into Europe. Indeed, recent days have had an air of unreality, with France and Germany signing a treaty of friendship. This action in itself could, of course, be a significant development provided it remains outward looking. The vision of a united Europe including the United Kingdom which has been presented by great statesmen in this century and which goes back to at least the days following the first world war, cannot lightly be set aside. One must stress the need for wider perspectives in pursuing this vision rather than short run pessimism because of difficulties in the Brussels negotiations.
Speaking as an individual I will say this. I regret that General de Gaulle and the government of France have felt it necessary to take the position they have with regard to participation by the United Kingdom, a position different from that of the other five member states of the European community.

From what the minister said I do not feel that there is on the part of the government a proper appreciation of the consequences of the failure of Britain to be in Europe what she has so much wanted to be in these last few months. Her failure to participate in the European common market will not mean the end of Britain or the end of Europe, but in my judgment it will certainly mark a very significant retreat in the opportunity of furthering peace in the world and unity among the western nations of the world. I greatly doubt whether the alternative which seems to be in the mind of the hon. gentleman is one that will have the significance underlined in the terms in which Mr. Churchill spoke when he advocated a united Europe. As to the conference which Canada and the United States have helped to cosponsor, I think he exaggerated the contribution made by this government. It should not be forgotten that well over a year before the invitation was extended and long before the prime ministers' conference in London last September, preparatory meetings for this conference had taken place elsewhere.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is not so.

The Prime Minister says that is not so. He will have an opportunity of showing why it is not so. However, I say that if he will look at the facts and will get properly briefed, he will see that what I have said represents the situation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Not at all.

The Secretary of State for External Affairs, after talking about this world economic conference, spoke of the desirability of the United States not getting tough with its allies. Of course, as I said a moment ago, we all recognize the fact that if the western alliance is to remain strong it must be, in fact and in truth, a real alliance of free nations. Each nation must be given the opportunity to express its views and make its influence felt.
I am going to say this to the minister and in doing so I have no pointed reference to any particular individual when I make the observation. I suspect that one of the tests, in diplomatic effort, of a nation's capacity to have a sphere of influence and to be persuasive, is so to comport oneself and so to formulate and execute the foreign policy of one's country so as to invite the kind of confidence among one's colleague states which will guarantee the preservation of that kind of freedom and of that kind of desired influence. I believe that in this context a disservice will be done and has been done

to the nation by the use of foreign policy as a means of furthering political ends in this or any other country.
In this context I might as well come to a subject that was referred to by the minister when he spoke of the attempts made by this government to bring home to the nations of the world the dangers of Soviet imperialism. No one denies that the subjugation of the free peoples of the world by the Soviet union is abhorrent to us all. No free man or woman in any part of the world can justify the subjugation by the Soviet union of the people of Poland, of the Ukraine, of Czechoslovakia, of Hungary and of other nations. All of us are agreed on this. However, the Prime Minister has sought-and I must say that the Secretary of State for External Affairs today seemed to do the same thing-to give the impression that not until this government came into office had any real advocacy by the government of Canada been made on behalf of these people, or not until the right hon. gentleman and his colleagues came into office. This is not the case. The present Leader of the Opposition, as secretary of state for external affairs in Canada, as leader of this party, as president of the United Nations general assembly and as chairman of the political committee in the United Nations, on many occasions spoke of the dangers of Soviet imperialism. I do not need to put on the record all the things he has said. His observations are to be found in the reports of the United Nations deliberations. They are to be found in the report of the deliberations of this house. However, I single out one because I well remember its being uttered in the United Nations general assembly when the Leader of the Opposition addressed himself to the then Soviet delegate, namely Andrei Vyshinsky. These are the words of the member for Algoma East speaking as secretary of state for external affairs on September 26, 1949, in the general assembly:
Imperialism of the old kind is a rapidly diminishing force-a dying doctrine. The real danger today lies in the new imperialism of the post-war period. During that period only one state in the world has extended its borders and the area of its domination. That state has annexed 179,000 square miles of territory and included within its borders in the last ten years more than twenty-one million people. Backed by its armies, it has imposed satellite regimes on neighbouring states. It has used its great material power and resources to rivet its economic control over the peoples under its influence. Its leaders have talked freely of "liberation" and of "national sovereignty", but its agents abroad have never hesitated to proclaim their obedience to its control and their determination to serve its interests above the interests of their own governments and their own peoples.
How can there be a feeling of peace and security-
Supply-External Affairs Said the Leader of the Opposition of today.
-where an alien power insists on imposing its domination over other nations and peoples?
We of the free democracies-
And when he said this, I am sure he spoke for everyone in this house, for everyone in this country and for all free peoples all over the world.
-reject this new imperialism which uses the subversive forces of international communism to destroy the national independence of even communist states which will not accept its interference and its dictates.
We also find at pages 1628 and following in Hansard, volume 2 for the last session, 1962, other statements placed on the records of this house, declarations made by former prime ministers who preceded this present government, and by the present Leader of the Opposition in several capacities, as secretary of state for external affairs and president of the United Nations general assembly. I am not saying that what the hon. gentleman said would not be supported by the Prime Minister or by others in this house. Indeed, I know that all hon. gentlemen in this house would support a statement such as the one I have quoted. But the significance of this turn in the debate is that the Prime Minister in particular has sought to convey the impression, as I sought to emphasize a few moments ago, that he alone and this government alone are to be regarded among the Canadian people as the political power in this country that has spoken up on behalf of the people in Europe who have been denied their freedom, because of Soviet union domination. Such is not the case.
I support the statement made by the right hon. gentleman in the general assembly of the United Nations in September of 1957. He made a speech there that won acclaim in the United Nations and in Canada. It was a statement that expressed in proper terms the views of the government of Canada and its people with regard to the denial of freedom by the Soviet union to millions of people in enslaved Europe. That was a speech of the highest order delivered by the Prime Minister. I took occasion in this house shortly thereafter to commend him for it. But what the Prime Minister said on that occasion, it should in fairness be noted, had been said on many occasions by Mr. St. Laurent and by the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson).

I thank the house for this concession. But this is not the end of the story. In the fall of 1961 the Prime Minister made a speech before a large gathering of Canadians with European origins. He spoke then as he had spoken in the general assembly of the United Nations in September of 1957. He spoke of the subjugation and enslavement of the peoples of certain European countries. The people who heard him applauded, quite properly, because he indicated further the concern of the government and the people of Canada. This was early in the month of November, I think. At any rate, it was while the general assembly of 1961 was in session. The Prime Minister said that as an earnest of what he was telling them the government was going to introduce in the United Nations general assembly in 1962 a resolution, calling upon the United Nations to condemn the Soviet union for acts of enslavement of human beings in many countries.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: With the support of like-minded nations in the United Nations.

Well, obviously you cannot pass a resolution unless you have the support of a sufficient number of nations. But I am suggesting to the Prime Minister that if he will look at the texts, and I have them all here-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is fine.
-he will find that when he made that speech he did not say anything at that time about the support of other nations.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Just read it.
The Prime Minister can do so when he speaks.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am just giving the hon. gentleman the facts.

What I have said will be supported by the newspapers, and in this instance I want the Prime Minister to know that I propose to make my own speech. Two days after the Prime Minister spoke I had occasion to speak at a gathering where I commended the Prime Minister for the course he had taken. But I urged him, if he thought it was desirable in order to achieve results, of the necessity of making friends in the United Nations, of providing a really effective solution, if these were the conditions and that was his wish, not to wait
[The Deputy Chairman.]

until the general assembly of 1962. As head of the government and in concert with his colleagues, why not give instructions at once to the Canadian delegation at the general assembly to bring in a resolution in 1961? That could have been done but it was not done.
Then we had the general election. I well remember the speech made by the Prime Minister in Neepawa, I think it was. It was a speech which he later corrected, particularly as to words attributed to him and as applied to the Leader of the Opposition. But the Winnipeg Free Press of May 11, and this is supported by the Toronto Telegram of the same date, reported him as follows:
Mr. Diefenbaker promised that next fall he would present a resolution to the United Nations asking the Soviet union to give freedom to the "captive peoples".
Certainly there is no reference there to having the support of a sufficient number of nations in the United Nations.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It was used all the time.

The Toronto
Telegram of May 23 reported the Prime
Minister as saying:
The Prime Minister also announced that Canada plans to enlist the support of other nations in introducing a resolution at the next United Nations general assembly calling for self-determination for the captive people in iron curtain countries.
And so on. This was repeated in several places throughout the campaign for one obvious purpose. I charge the Prime Minister that it was done for the obvious purpose of seeking to influence certain people to support the government in respect of a matter on which the Prime Minister knew perfectly well there was no division whatsoever as between political parties in this country.
The general assembly of 1962 has terminated its sessions, but there was no resolution put forward by the Canadian government or by the Prime Minister. He said at one point he was going to go there himself. In the Montreal Gazette of August 23, 1962 he is reported as follows:
Prime Minister Diefenbaker indicated yesterday he may go to the United Nations general assembly session in New York late next month to sponsor a resolution calling for free elections in Soviet satellite countries.
Then there is this very interesting addendum:
He told reporters he would consider doing so if Premier Khrushchev attends the general assembly meeting, but at the moment reports of the Russian leader's plans are contradictory.
I simply want to say to the Prime Minister that while he holds a very important office I doubt very much that the decision of Mr. Khrushchev to go to the United Nations

depended upon the convenience of the present Prime Minister of Canada. In any event, there was no resolution presented. The parliamentary secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs made a speech. It was a good speech. I would expect him to make a good speech. But what he said in substance, I am sure he will agree, was the same in principle as was stated by the Prime Minister in the general assembly in 1957 and by the Leader of the Opposition and by Mr. St. Laurent and others at the United Nations over the years.
I say to the Prime Minister that there is a lot of talk these days about the commitments of a nation to other governments. This was a particular commitment by the Prime Minister to the people of Canada and it was not discharged.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It was always subject to getting the necessary support of other like-minded nations.

The Secretary of State for External Affairs spoke again today of disarmament. I must say the minister did not have the same confidence in the outcome of nuclear test ban and disarmament discussions which has characterized the other speeches he has made on these subjects in this house, since he became Secretary of State for External Affairs. The minister, I am sure, now recognizes that the solution of the problem of disarmament is not as easy as he thought in the early period of his ministry. We all support disarmament. We must continue to negotiate with the Soviet union and, ultimately with communist China, and with all countries, in an effort to have a system of disarmament that will minimize the possibilities of war by miscalculation.
Let there be no mistake about our support for this objective, all of us in this house and all of us in this country. This we can do, however, in this difficult nuclear age, only provided there is an agreement accompanied by the assurance of fulfilment of that agreement with regard to the measures of control which must be mutually agreed upon, not only control measures and inspection, but agreement as to what the objectives of control are.
Now, the minister seems to think that there is some ground for hope as a result of a recent exchange of letters between the Soviet union and the United States concerning on-site inspections. He looks upon this as an encouraging reason for believing that there may be some progress in this area. Let us hope that there is. I can only remind the hon. gentleman that Mr. Arthur Dean, for whom I know the minister has the highest regard and to whom he paid a tribute the other day, shortly before retiring as United States spokesman in the
Supply-External Affairs nuclear test discussions, did not express the view which the minister has expressed here. He did express the view, however, with regard to disarmament, that while every effort must be made to bring about some agreement in this vital field, it was not doing any service to mankind to overstate the possibilities or to be guilty of exaggerated optimism.
I have read with very considerable interest, as perhaps the minister has, a book that has just been published by Mr. James Wadsworth who, under three presidents, represented the United States in the disarmament discussions. Here is what he said, among other things:
There is a very real question whether genuine disarmament is possible at all in the continued presence of critical political situations like Berlin. Many experts believe, and I concur, that a significant and durable relaxation of the cold war is a prime prerequisite to any relaxation of the arms race.
I think it is not a mature position to take to say that we are going to achieve disarmament in the light of the existence of the very serious differences that yet prevail between the disputants in matters of major political importance. We all hope it will be otherwise. I would not want the leader of the N.D.P. party to conclude, as the hon. member for Kootenay West has on other occasions with regard to this kind of observation, that there was not on my part the fullest appreciation of the desirability of making progress in disarmament. Of course, we must all work towards this objective. My point is that we will not reach that objective if we continue to overlook the realities involved in the present international situation.
The minister mentioned, as an indication of the recognition of the worth of Canada in these consultations, the fact that we had been selected as one of the members of the 10-power disarmament committee. We were selected by the four foreign ministers who met to set up this body. Well, I am sure that we are all proud of the fact that the contribution of Canada has been such that it has warranted the selection of this country to serve in the current disarmament discussions. However, I would remind the minister that in 1954 Canada was a member of the subcommittee on disarmament, the five members of which were the United States, France, Great Britain, the Soviet union and Canada. Canada was selected by the United Nations generally to represent all the other nations. I think that marks us as having warranted at that time the very tribute which the minister wants to take, and I think properly so, for his government and for Canada. We were on that subcommittee. It was Canada that was selected to carry on negotiations on behalf of the other four with the Soviet union concerning the conditions that must prevail if

Supply-External Affairs there was to be a resumption of disarmament discussions. Let it not be suggested, therefore, as the minister sought to imply today, that only this government is interested in disarmament. No one worked harder for disarmament under equally difficult circumstances than did the Leader of the Opposition, just as I frankly acknowledge the minister, himself, has worked diligently and hard towards this objective during his term of office. I simply say to the minister, it is one thing to work hard but it is another thing to work wisely in this field. I do not think it is possible to work wisely unless we take into account the existence of the fundamental differences in ideology that prevail between the Soviet union and the free world, the existence of major political problems that divide east and west.
We will reach, I hope, a stage where we can have at least partial agreement on disarmament under conditions that will not violate our security. But it is not mature, it seems to me at this time, to overstate the possibility or the extent of progress made thus far.
Now, Mr. Chairman, one striking fact it seems to me in international affairs today is the interrelatedness of a nation's defence policy, its foreign economic policy and its over-all policy. These three areas which in the past we have tended to look upon separately, now must be considered all together. Indeed, the continuous nature of this interrelatedness has major implications, as I see it, for our own foreign policy, particularly in the area of planning and co-ordinating of our own efforts and our own policies. Perhaps we should be considering some alterations. Do we have over-all planning and co-ordination of effort in the government at the present time which gives its total attention to a particular problem in external relations and is continually casting its eye up and down the radar screen looking for problems in areas where Canada can exert an influence?
The diplomatic influence and effectiveness of a nation is a total process, a composite whole, in which our political conduct, the state of our alliances, the amount of foreign assistance which we give, our military power, our domestic economic situation, operate all together. It is a truism that Canadian diplomatic influence and effectiveness must be less than what it could be when our own internal economic affairs are in a state of confusion and when our nation appears to be doubly confused and without a vigorous national purpose.
Many commentators in recent years have noted that Canada seems to have less "effect in international affairs than formerly. They say we do not possess the power and influence

we once did. The minister knows who say this. I am not saying it, but I can refer, as the minister knows, to those objective assessments which have been made of the government's foreign policy, to the way they have executed it; I cannot absolve the government from blame in this matter. Indeed, as has been so often commented on, our diplomacy has been a great deal less than satisfactory in a number of areas, and there are other reasons as well for our present situation.
The fact is that in today's world the pace of change has become so rapid as to destroy utterly the process of gradualism which we had once come to know. Revolutionary change has become a part of our lives, and yet we have not adjusted our thinking to the implications of the scientific and technological revolution of our times.
We need to be constantly re-examining our foreign policy objectives, constantly querying the means by which these objectives are carried out. The minister today said we have begun a new era. Well, if we are in a new era surely we are entitled to have, particularly at a time when we are discussing national defence, a statement on it as well as on our foreign policy objectives, how we pursue them and how they are related to defence and international commercial policies. This is necessary if we are to have a mature consideration of our foreign policy.
Now, Mr. Chairman, before I resume my seat I say to the minister, as I have often said to him on other occasions in these debates, we endeavour in this country, and I think properly so, to minimize the occasion when we have to differ with the government on foreign policy. We basically support the same principles, although because of what the minister said today it seems to me that in this new era there is a need for a re-enunciation of those principles and new adaptations, if we are to satisfy fully the obligations of this debate.
The government, this party and other parties in the house are not basically divided on the broad lines of foreign policy. Therefore, in the consideration of these matters, let us not be afraid to express our differences. Let us not be afraid to point out where there are weaknesses. Let us not exaggerate our achievements whether in terms of collective effort or in terms of national achievement, but let us bear in mind that in this difficult period there must be stated goals of foreign policy carefully adhered to, respected by all branches of the government, the defence department as well as the Department of External Affairs.
Differences between ministers or differences of policy with regard to ministers in these

departments are not conducive to the development of a strong and respected position for this country in the United Nations or elsewhere in the world. So I say to the minister we must pay more attention to our long run objectives and to policies and ways by which we can continue to play an effective role in foreign policy. The minister has that opportunity and I submit to him with the greatest respect that that obligation was not discharged by him today.

Mr. Chairman, we have listened to a partial statement by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and we have listened to today's spokesman for the Liberal party on the same subject. I am more than ever convinced that it is time we came to grips with all of the basic issues concerning external affairs and defence. We have avoided decisions long enough. Canadians want to be informed. They want action, not talk.
I shall not take time this afternoon to review world developments. That has already been done. Rather I shall endeavour to get down to what I regard as some of the major issues that are before us. During the past few weeks the question of Canada's military policy, and this is very definitely related to the over-all picture of external affairs, has come prominently before the public, and Canadians have become properly concerned about the attitudes of their politicians and alarmed at the general situation relating to Canada's role in the international scene.
The politicians of our old line parties have much to answer for to the electorate of Canada. Surely, however, nothing condemns the weakness of both the government and the Liberal party in the face of urgent threatening problems so much as the total failure of both to state clearly their policies on nuclear weapons for a period of something like three years, except perhaps to accuse each other of what the other has not done or, if done, has done wrong? It is no wonder the Canadian people have become confused. It is no wonder, because there has been no clear light for them to follow.
Canada's weapons policy at the present time is a matter of urgent public importance. Perhaps we only now realize how serious was the Cuban crisis last October and how totally unprepared we were to take effective action. If this crisis has driven politicians in all parties to come to some decision on this important question then perhaps indeed it has done some good. Events do not wait on us forever, and through lack of decision our freedom can easily be lost. If we look back it is not difficult to see that the government has in fact committed us to a policy whereby, if we had no nuclear arms, we had no effective weapons for defence at all.

The CF-104 and the Voodoo aircraft, the Honest John rocket launcher and the Bomarc missile were all designed for maximum effect with nuclear warheads. Their empty mouths mock us if we do not arm them as they were intended to be armed; yet now we learn the Bomarc is no longer to be used by the United States. In fact it has rapidly become obsolete altogether. The government of Canada has at no time admitted it had a nuclear policy. Rather we have had the pathetic spectacle of our minister of external affairs respected as the apostle of disarmament and negotiated peace at the United Nations while, at the same time, the Minister of National Defence travels about the country and the world telling us we need nuclear weapons, and all the while the Prime Minister of this country sits in between remaining evasive and uncommitted. It is no wonder the Canadian people are confused.
On the other hand the leader of the Liberal party can hardly be proud that it took him three years of shilly-shallying to come down at last to a recognizable position on nuclear policy. He is a winner of the Nobel peace prize, a man known to be one of the best versed Canadians in the field of foreign affairs, a man who should know, if anyone knows in this country, the ins and outs of NATO policies and our commitments and our responsibilities to our allies. He is the man who hopes one day to become prime minister of this country.
How long has this man been evading his responsibility of bringing to the people of Canada a clear statement of policy regarding the question of nuclear armament? I ask him to state just what are our commitments to NATO and to NORAD. I would like to know. Or does he know? I think it was Mark Twain who once said that it is always good to know the facts before you twist them. Did the Cuban crisis and the developing political situation force him to announce a decision? Perhaps it was on the advice of the former commander of NATO, General Norstad. Or was it another instance of political expediency? Why have not the Liberals advocated before today Canada joining the organization of American states?
They have.

Why did they not do so when they were in government because, as the previous speaker has stated, the invitation to join the organization of American states has been there for many, many years. This is why I believe that today Canada needs leadership, a statement of what is its policy and what are the facts as they relate

Supply-External Affairs not only to our commitments but to our responsibility, to our people, to our nation and to our friends and allies.
We are at war with communism. The war is not a "hot" war at the present time. Pray God that it never will become that. It is a war, none the less. It is the expressed determination of the leaders of communist nations to force their will and their way of life on the free nations of the world. It was Khrushchev himself who said, "We will bury you"-and he means just that. He now thinks it can be done without the use of nuclear conflict, but the Chinese communists have other ideas. They mutually agree, though, on the subversion of our institutions and our government by infiltration, by economic techniques-yes, and by destroying our will to resist. This is the greatest danger that threatens us in this war, because brainwashing as far as the communists are concerned is nothing more or less than a method of destroying the will to resist. Certainly we can hardly expect to peacefully co-exist with men who deny and reject the moral laws which we accept and by which we live. The leaders of communism make no attempt to conceal this fact. The problem is simply that we refuse to hear, or if we hear, we refuse to understand.
In the face of reality I suggest that there are three alternatives before us. One is that we become neutral; second, that we join the forces of the east in this ideological struggle; third, that we join the forces of the west. Now just let us look at this simply. Neutrality does not pay. In fact, there is no dogma, there is no intolerance so intolerant as neutralism. Certainly Canada has no part, nor do Canadians have any part, in neutrality. It took a long time for Mr. Nehru to wake up to this fact, but he now has. It is impossible for us to join the opposite side in this cold war. If we stop for a moment and recognize the heritage that is ours in this free land of ours, certainly these are the things that we ought to hold most dear, and there can be no place for us whatever on the other side. Therefore we are put without equivocation on the side of the free world, and as one of the larger of the small nations we must stand with our friends; we must stand on those principles which we know are true and then, when all has been done, stand again. This is our responsibility and it is only in the light of this that we can actually face up to the problems that we have.
Mr. Krushchev in speaking to the world
has made it very clear that he is against nuclear wars. His reason for saying this is simply that he knows that in a nuclear war

no one could emerge a victor and that both sides would be destroyed. Instead he favours war of his own design that will speed the day of the communist take-over. He promises to support the inevitable revolutionary wars such as we now have in Laos. He calls these wars "people's wars", wars of liberation; he calls them sacred wars. He has not changed his opinion on that. They are inspired and led by the communists themselves. He intends to abolish the occupation regime in Berlin, as the dividing wall has already told us. The new front of active struggle centering in Cuba is regarded as something which all communists regard as a duty to support. Let us not think that just because a few missiles have been taken away from Cuba the danger in Cuba has disappeared. All one has to do is read the newspapers of today or yesterday to understand that. Nevertheless, where the transition to communism can be accomplished by peaceful means, no war is desired. Otherwise communists must encourage armed uprising and civil war. They believe capitalism is doomed and is declining in power and prestige. That communism is the invincible force of our age is their basic conviction. Mr. Chairman, may I call it five o'clock?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I realize that this is private members' hour but I wonder whether the house would agree to revert to motions in order to permit me to make an announcement regarding the Atlantic development board. It will only take a very short time.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Prime Minister seeks the unanimous consent of the house to revert to motions. Is that agreed?
