speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I thank the house. I wish to announce the appointment of the chairman and members of the Atlantic development board. Hon. members know that this board is being established under an act passed earlier in the session and will have the responsibility of investigating and reporting upon measures and projects for fostering the economic growth and development of the Atlantic region.

The chairman of the board will be Brigadier J. Michael S. Wardell of Fredericton, New Brunswick, the publisher of the daily Gleaner and also that well known monthly magazine The Atlantic Advocate. Mr. Wardell has been tremendously interested in expanding the economy of the Atlantic provinces. The other four members of the board will be Mr. Frank H. Sobey of Stellarton, Nova Scotia; Mr. Melvin McQuaid of Souris, Prince Edward Island; Mr. Fred Ayre of St. John's, Newfoundland; and Mr. Donat LaLande of Moncton, New Brunswick. Mr. Sobey is the chairman of Sobey's Stores Limited of Stellarton; chairman of the United Steel Corporation Limited; and president of Industrial Estates Limited. He is also a director of a number of firms, including Maritime Steel and Foundries Limited, Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation Limited, the Nova Scotia Trust Company, and so forth.
Mr. Melvin McQuaid is a well known public figure in Prince Edward Island, who from 1958 to 1962 was provincial treasurer and attorney and advocate general of that province. Mr. Fred Ayre of St. John's, Newfoundland, is managing director of Bowring Bros. Limited, one of the largest, if not the largest, merchandising establishments in Newfoundland, with branches in Labrador, Halifax, Nova Scotia, and Montreal, Quebec.
Mr. Donat LaLande of Moncton, New Brunswick, is the assistant general manager of the maritime district, Provincial Bank of Canada, who has also throughout the years devoted himself to the welfare of the maritime provinces.
The act provides that members of the board are appointed to hold office for a term of five years, except that of those first appointed one shall be appointed for three years and two shall be appointed for four years. Accordingly, the term of the chairman and Mr. Sobey will run for five years, that of Mr. McQuaid and Mr. Ayre for four years, and that of Mr. LaLande for three years. The government is very appreciative of the fact that these five outstanding representatives of the Atlantic region have agreed to serve as the first directors of this important new institution.

Mr. Speaker, whatever our views have been of the legislation, I am sure that everyone in the house will be glad that this board has now been appointed. speechtext:
The house in committee on Bill SD-5, for the relief of Marion Ruth Catherine Slattery -Mr. Mandziuk-Mr. Paul in the chair.
On clause 1-Marriage dissolved.

Mr. Chairman, we are being asked today to grant a divorce to Marion Ruth Catherine Slattery, who lives in the city of Montreal. We note that in this case the people concerned are quite young. They have been separated and there has been a history of some disagreement. We also note that there is a rather unique feature in the bill in that the investigators are not the normal class of investigator but are related to the petitioner. As in all cases where there are investigators and where investigation must be proven, I think there is also a desire to give more credence to the evidence of those who are not interested for financial reasons in the case. But where there are blood relations involved there are other interests which must also be given consideration.
In this case it seems to me that we must look at the evidence. I think it is important to look at the questions asked. The questions commence on page 2, and I should like to point out that in reading the evidence I found that the barrister-at-law from Montreal in my opinion did a very good job and asked the questions in a way in which I think they should be asked. I certainly would commend his handling of the case to other lawyers who I think have not done as well.

Divorce Bills
The questions start in this way:
Q. Mrs. Slattery, were you born in Montreal?
A. Yes.
Q. Have you lived there all your life?
A. Yes.
Q. Was your husband bom in Montreal?
A. Yes.
Q. Has he lived there all his life?
A. Yes.
Q. Is he still living in Montreal, to your knowledge?
A. Yes.
Q. Is he employed in Montreal?
A. Yes.
Q. Do you know the firm for which he works?
A. The Weekend Picture Magazine.
Q. Do you know how long he has been employed by that company?
A. About 10 years.
Q. So far as you know does he intend to remain in Montreal, Canada?
A. Yes.
Mr. Chairman, I think that in this case counsel has established the matter of domicile in a straightforward way and has asked the questions which are sometimes not asked, but which in this case have been well presented.
Then the chairman asked:
Q. How old is your husband?

Then Mr. Greenberg continued:
Q. Did you cohabit with your husband and live as man and wife after you were married?
A. Yes.
Q. Were there any children born of your marriage?
A. No.
Q. How many times have you separated from your husband?
A. Twice.
Q. When was the first occasion?
A. In June of 1959.
Q. What were the immediate causes of that separation?
A. He was constantly going away on week ends by himself, and when I asked him to explain his absence he wouldn't tell me and he didn't treat me very well, so I went to my mother's.
Q. When was this?
A. In June of 1959.
Mr. Chairman, you will notice that the difficulty which developed in this marriage developed after the marriage had been in effect for something like three years. Mr. Chairman, if you would give some consideration to a suggestion which has been made by many hon. members in this committee which is in the form of a bill now before the house, it would seem to me that if a court was handling this particular case and had been available to this couple, in view of the fact that this marriage had a reconciliation feature about it and the marriage had been in effect for three years, if family counselling had been available this is probably one of the cases which would not have come before us. If we are going to continue as we appear

to be continuing and to operate as a pseudocourt, if we were to establish for ourselves the services of a family court, which would have all the machinery available to such an institution, which would allow for the assistance and the rendering of advice to this particular couple during the period when the marriage was already in jeopardy, when there had been a temporary separation and the marriage was later resumed, then it seems to me this marriage might have been saved.
It seems to me that as a court we should have the right and the obligation to suggest whenever it seems advantageous that assistance be made available, and be made available by competent people on the instruction of the appropriate court, in order to see that a reconciliation of the marriage is attempted and is worked for. Because it is generally assumed, I think correctly so, that the institution of marriage, lying in the public domain, is of public interest and therefore the public has an obligation to see that the element of matrimony is maintained at as high a degree as possible. I think this can be accomplished in many cases by the use of a family court and the machinery which would be available for counselling services.
After the second reconciliation took place the wife returned to her husband. She had lived at her mother's house for the period of her separation which was of very short duration, namely four or five days and she had returned to her husband. Fortunately in this case, while the couple were quite young and probably ill advised in some of their actions, the mother of the girl insisted that the couple return and after four or five days had persuaded her daughter to go back to the husband. The questioning continues as follows:
Q. How were things after you went back? A. For a while they were fine and then in November, 1959, he started the same things again, going away week ends by himself and he wouldn't explain his absence. When I asked him why he didn't take me he said, "If you want to go out, go out. I don't care what you do".
I think this is an indication that if the services I mentioned had been available at that time we might not be considering this case today. There was a period of time in which the marriage had actually been reentered upon successfully and not much objection was taking place at the time. The questioning continues:
Q. Did you have regular quarrels after these week ends of absence? A. Yes.
Q. Did he treat you badly during these quarrels? A. Yes.
Q. What did you do after this? A. When I would ask him where he was he wouldn't answer me and he pushed me aside and told me not to bother him. I would ask him, "Where were you? Where have you been?" And on one occasion he grabbed me and tried to choke me and he said, "Look, don't bother me. It's none of your business where I go."

Q. When was the occasion of your second and final separation? A. In May of 1960.
Q. How did that come about, exactly? A. He was away for the whole week end. On the Saturday night I was afraid to stay by myself because the people in the building were away. I was alone in the building.
Q. What did you do? A. I went down to my mother's place on Saturday night.
Q. Did you try to communicate with your husband during the week end? A. Yes. I phoned him all week end and I couldn't reach him until the evening of Sunday night.
Q. What happened when you reached him at that time? A. I called him and all I said to him was, "I am at my mother's". And he said, "Good, stay there".
Q. Have you lived with him since that time? A. No, I haven't.
Q. You have stayed with your mother since that date? A. Yes.
Q. What did you do the next day, Monday? A. I left the next day. I went home and took some of my clothing with me and I went back to my mother.

(Text):

Thank you, Mr. Chairman, for your guidance. I should like to say that I am not reading entirely from the evidence. You also have my assurance that I am not reading from a speech. I have the original certified copy of the transcript of the actual evidence from the other place and it is certainly not a speech, although these transcripts may be a collection of speeches by barristers, senators, petitioners, respondents and various other witnesses.
I think that to paraphrase some of the evidence would not be a fair way to present the case. Unfortunately many members of the house do not get the evidence and I should not like to give an improper presentation of the evidence by paraphrasing rather than referring directly to it. However, you have my assurance that it is not a speech I have here but rather the transcript of evidence obtained from the other place.
As I was pointing out, in this particular case there was considerable opportunity to do something if the circumstances had been right, and in referring to the evidence and making some comment on it I should like to say that I think it highlights our inability to assist these people when assistance is needed most.
Hon. members will notice from the evidence that in 1962 the respondent was 25 years old and that the marriage took place on June 16, 1956 when she was only 19 years old. While she was of the age of legal consent, I believe we leave to chance many times the obligations we have under the matrimonial causes act. There is little education along this line and I think that we may have failed in this case to take advantage of what I believe was an obvious opportunity for the operation of marriage counselling services. It may be, and rightly so, that in many cases it is a responsibility of the faiths to which these people belong to provide this type of counselling. I am sure that in many cases this is done and that advice along this line is provided.
However, I think it would be advisable for us to consider certain points in looking at a case of this kind. The marriage took place in 1956 and it was 1959 before trouble developed. The marriage staggered along until the spring of 1961 when there was a final break-up. It seems to me that there was

an opportunity in this case for some type of family counselling. The British North America Act has given us the right to do these things and to make regulations and laws, and I would point out that I have already placed a bill before the house which would accomplish this end if it were adopted.
The very serious problem which developed here and which resulted in this young lady coming to parliament and asking for a divorce from her husband could quite possibly have been eliminated, particularly in the period from May, 1960 to 1961 when the marriage Anally broke up. It is unfortunate in this case that the necessity arose of presenting such evidence as is found in the latter part of the transcript. There is evidence that the marriage which took place on June 16, 1956 was consummated but there were no children.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired. I have given him additional time because of the points of order that were raised.
Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

In rising to speak on this bill, I want to say that I do so reluctantly. This afternoon in the house we have been talking about matters of world-wide importance, matters concerning all the countries of the world, problems relating to the survival of mankind, peace and war, and now at Ave o'clock the whole machinery of the House of Commons grinds to a stop. These great matters of world-wide importance are set aside and we begin to discuss the problems of divorce.
I have read the evidence in this particular case. It is a well documented case. There is no reason why it should not go through. Everything appears to be in order, and I hope that the committee will pass the bill this afternoon. As I say, I am reluctant to speak on it at all. It is unfortunate we could not ask for the unanimous consent of the house to continue discussing the world-wide problems that were before us. Indeed, to me it is a tragedy that these items are pushed aside while we consider matters of this kind.
I do hope that during this session some action will be taken by the members of the house so that we will not continually be put in this absurd and tragic position.

While I agree with what the hon. member for Danforth has said, I think it should be pointed out that the members of this house have taken unto themselves the responsibility for adjudicating upon each case. Since that has been done, I believe we are going to have to And some new way of doing this. If I were to adjudicate on this case,
Divorce Bills
I would say that I agree with the hon. member for Danforth when he says that this is
a good case.
However, Mr. Chairman, I think this case has the same problem attached to it as all other cases have which come before us. We have to look at this evidence very closely because we are setting ourselves up as a quasi court. I am prepared to study this case and bring some matters to the attention of the committee. I believe we should consider the evidence as carefully as we do in any other case. In looking through the evidence I notice that the lawyer very carefully and skilfully leads the witness through a number of questions in order to establish certain facts. I am wondering if the same evidence would have been given if the witness had been allowed to make her own presentation rather than just answer questions. It seems to me that in this case the lawyer handled it very well. He asked questions such as these:
Q. Did you have regular quarrels after these week ends of absence?
A. Yes.
Q. Did he treat you badly during these quarrels? A. Yes.
Q. What did you do after this?
A. When I would ask him where he was he wouldn't answer me and he pushed me aside and told me not to bother him. I would ask him, "Where were you? Where have you been?" And on one occasion he grabbed me and tried to choke me and he said, "Look, don't bother me. It's none of your business where I go".
In reading this evidence it would appear that they had a nice quarrel, a very quiet quarrel. You might as well have said, "After you Alphonse". It seems to me the language does not indicate the fact that the young lady has been choked; he says, "Look, don't bother me." It seems to me the questioning is rather leading.
We come now in this case to the establishment of the charge of adultery, and I think this is fairly important. I should like the hon. member for Danforth, if time is available, to say something on the legal aspects of a problem we have here. This problem is indicated by these questions and answers:
Q. Mrs. Slattery, what has happened since that time to lead you to believe that your husband hai been living with another woman?
A. Well, he lives in the same area in Verdun as I do and I saw him in his car with another woman and they had a little baby in the car with them.
Q. Did you recognize this other woman?
A. Yes I knew her from the area.
Q. Are you personally acquainted with her?
A. No.
Q. Do you know her name?
A. Yes.
Q. What is her name?
A. Joan Tibbo.

Divorce Bills
Q. On this occasion when you say you saw her with your husband in his car with the little baby did you inquire about this?
A. Yes, I did.
If the hon. gentleman wishes to carry on a conversation, I hope he will speak a little louder. Now, I am only annoyed by the mut-terings but I would be quite happy to answer a question if he wants to ask one.
I am just helping you to kill time.

I would be very happy to have the hon. member discuss this case if he sees fit.
I would make this point. The evidence given establishes that, before the divorce procedure was set up, the true reason for the divorce is established rather than the adultery charge which is dealt with later. I should like the hon. member for Danforth to consider the fact that, here is a woman who presumes her husband is living with another woman who has a child. This, in itself, would be fairly strong evidence that adultery had been committed. It does not seem as though any effort has been made to hide the fact that there is a child. I believe, therefore, that the basis of this case is a common law arrangement, which is not necessarily an adulterous arrangement; but in a case where a child is born adultery would be presumed.
I believe this would be the grounds in this case rather than the grounds established in the evidence. I feel that this is a technical point. I notice, too, that there is an interest on the part of the wife herself who did not go out and hire lawyers to get the evidence that must be produced before this tribunal. My point is that I do not believe we should go through all the procedures since there appear to be grounds established in the early part of the evidence that are more legitimate than the grounds that are developed later in the evidence.
I believe the fact that she is commonly accepted as his wife in that part of the community, of having a child accepted by him in that part of the community, and of establishing a common law domicile habitation in that area should establish the grounds for divorce, and not the grounds that are later developed. These grounds involve the brother of the girl and her mother. Maybe the committee would be interested in what happened. They go to the house, and it is interesting to note that again the mother comes in. She seems to be a very intelligent woman and says that the daughter should take a trip and go on holidays to think the matter over very seriously before she does anything about it. On returning

from the holiday the mother and daughter both go to see a lawyer to get information about how to get a divorce.
This is the part that seems to me rather foolish, that in normal circumstances the establishment and non-denial of the establishment of a common law marriage in itself should not be an acceptable ground before this committee. It is quite true that we have not amended the Canada divorce act, that we have in it only provision for divorce on the grounds of adultery, but it seems to me there should be an amendment to the rules in the other place to allow for a divorce on the grounds of cohabitation with someone other than the marriage partner. This should be very easily established if there is an issue of that common law union.
In this case the normal procedure is gone through. The brother, the wife and the mother go to the apartment of the husband and they enter it. Incidentally she decided that she was not going to go there but she said she discussed it with her lawyer.
Q. Did you inquire about anything else with Mr. Rohrick at this time?
A. Yes, I told him I had been trying to get some personal things and my husband wouldn't let me have them, and I said, "Can X go to the apartment and get them?"
Q. What personal things were these?
A. I had a portable sewing machine I wanted and some crystal I bought before I got married.
Q. And your husband wouldn't give you these things?
A. No, and he said he would have me arrested if I went to the house because I had left on my own accord.
Q. Did you still have the key to the apartment?
A. Yes.
Q. What did Mr. Rohrick tell you?
A. Mr. Rohrick said that he couldn't have me arrested, that I could go but he said, "You best bring somebody with you to witness that you are just taking what is yours."
Q. And did you do this?
A. Yes.
Incidentally, Mr. Chairman, this reminds me of the R.C.M.P. going into somebody's place just taking what is theirs, and doing so in many cases without what seems to be the proper advice being given.
Anyway, they arrive on Tuesday night, September 26, 1961 and she is accompanied by her brother and mother. They open the door with the key and the brother goes in first. They go into the bedroom and again there is the same kind of problem. Maybe, Mr. Chairman, this is only because they are not qualified detectives and have not had the experience of some other detectives; because in the whole shuffle-and I do not want to read it all-they missed the baby. In the contention I put forward the baby would be an important part of our consideration; but if you will notice they went into the house, the brother went down the hall and into the bedroom, and

the husband was at the door of the bedroom. The brother met him and while he was putting on a bathrobe over his pyjamas the question is asked:
Q. How many bedrooms were in that apartment?
A. Just one.
Q. In this bedroom was your husband alone?
A. No.
Q. Who was with him?
A. The same girl who was in the car with him.
Q. Miss Joan Tibbo?
A. Yes.
Q. Where was she?
A. She was in the bed.
Q. Do you recall the exact date of this visit to the apartment?
A. 26th September, 1961.
Q. Where was this Joan Tibbo?
A. She was in the bed too.
Q. How many beds were there in that room?
A. Just one.
Mr. Chairman, I wonder at this point what would happen if there were two beds in that room. What would the senators do in that particular case? Somebody says "Look under the bed." In this particular case the question was not asked if they looked under the bed. Maybe the committee would be interested some time in finding two beds in one bedroom to see what kind of situation would develop.
Q. What kind of a bed was it?
A. Double bed.
Q. What part of the bed was she in?
A. The side near the wall.
Q. Do you recall what she was wearing?
A. She had baby doll pyjamas on.
This may be the advisor to the other famous detective who always had the girls dressed in baby dolls. They may have been blue or pink but they were always baby dolls. Maybe it was not the detective who thought this up. Maybe it was the lawyer in the case who thought it up.
Shame.

Some lawyers have lots of imagination, I have found.
Q. Did you notice any articles of her clothing around the room?
A. Yes, there were some things showing on the chair, a slip and some other things.
A number of other questions follow which I do not think are of any importance and the question is asked:
Q. Could you tell whether the bed had been occupied by the two of them before you got there?
A. Yes, because there were marks on the pillows and the bed clothes were thrown back.
Q. What did you do then?
A. My brother said, "Let's get out of here", so we turned around and walked out.
I notice in walking out they did not take either the crystal or the sewing machine. They may have been excited. There may have been other things said but it surprises me that they did not stop for the sewing machine or crystal.
Divorce Bills
Q. You have not. of course, lived with your husband at all since that day?
A. No.
Q. Have you received any support financially from your husband since that day?
A. No.
They then go on to ask what she earns and then the chairman intervenes and said:
Deal with collusion and connivance.
I am very pleased to see that was done. This is something we could recommend to some of our provincial courts to deal with, so that judges would keep this in mind and refer to it.
By Mr. Greenberg:
Q. Has there been any collusion between your husband and yourself to obtain this divorce?
A. No.
By the Chairman:
Q. You know what that means?
A. Yes, I do.
Q. You have not made any arrangements with your husband to get this divorce?
A. I have not spoken to him.
Q. You have not connived at or planned the adultery in any way.
A. No.
Q. You have not condoned the adultery, forgiving your husband?
A. No.
The reason I believe this is very important is because of the fact that in a case like this it is quite likely that the young lady herself would decide that, and she has indicated there was no chance of reconciliation, and because there is no chance of reconciliation she really is getting the divorce on the basis of the common law marriage that is in effect. This is the point I would like the lawyers to consider, that in the legislative sense it would be much easier for us to say the divorce is being granted on the basis of the common law alliance rather than on this particular limited and very sketchy evidence which indicates absolutely nothing about adultery but that two people were together sleeping in this particular bed. I believe the adultery is much more clearly indicated in the common law alliance which has resulted in an issue, and at this point I would wish some of the legal pundits in this court would give it their consideration. Then Mr. Greenberg, the counsel, asked the question I was concerned with before:
Q. Would you take your husband back at this time?
A. No, not when there is a baby involved, I wouldn't.
By the Chairman:
Q. Was the baby in the room when you went in there?
A. It wasn't in the bedroom. The living room was in darkness so I don't know if it was there.
I wonder why she did not ask when she went to get the crystal and the sewing

Divorce Bills
machine. She might then have found out whether the baby was there. Mr. Chairman, while I agree that this is a good case and would probably go through in court, has adultery, in your able opinion, been proved in this case? Was the baby borrowed from one of the neighbours to create a situation which would set up this investigation? I would think that if the baby was there, if there was a baby in fact in the whole procedure, the common law alliance itself would of necessity have to be proved. The detectives in this case or, as it happened, the sleuths- the wife, the mother and the brother-should have scouted around and found out whether this baby was in fact living there. At this time the baby was probably old enough to be out and around. I suggest that is a very important part of the evidence.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, belief in a democracy does not necessarily mean hostility toward or enmity of different ideologies. Our nature as Canadians is to be tolerant. In the beginning we did not want to come to the point where we would counter communism with war and armed strife. We may even be loath to admit it now, but we must admit that deep in our hearts we recognize that there can be no conciliation between communism and western democracy, any more than darkness can be conciliated with light, or wrong with right. It is time that we admitted this openly. However, we cannot be so foolish as to believe that we can preserve our way of life by force alone. Particularly at this present time should we realize that armed force is no longer the only means by which a country can prevail over its enemies. On the other hand we must also realize that we can never prevail in our cause in this world struggle if we allow ourselves to be overwhelmed by the force of an enemy. Thus we Canadians face up to the reality of world crises and the inherent dangers which face us, even now at this particular time.
The cold war is not one of our own choosing. The Canadian people want nothing more than to live in peace-to live in peace with themselves and with their neighbours. But we are at war because communism is at war with us, and if we wish to preserve our way of life we must fight for it or it will be wrested away from us. It is our responsibility as politicians to lay these things clearly before our people. The Canadian people want to be told the dangers which face them. We all want to do our part in our humble stations to secure freedom and safety for ourselves, for our families and for our 27507-3-196
Supply-External Affairs country. Too much of the time our old line politicians take no decisive stand against this danger. Either they pooh-pooh it or else they pretend it is not there.
Since the end of world war II the free world has been pursuing a policy definitely designed to contain the communist menace. I believe this policy has been right, in spite of our government's indecisiveness at times. I believe we must stand for the way of life we believe in, one that respects the rights of an individual against the threat of a totalitarian government. I believe that if we are to win then we must adopt the best weapons at our disposal, and these are not military weapons alone. There can be no substitution for moral standards; let us never forget that.
To put the present situation in its proper perspective the over-all military picture must be considered from four aspects; from the moral aspect, from the economic aspect, from the political aspect, and from the strategic aspect. Let us look at the moral side of the picture first. In one sense Canada is already committed to nuclear arms. For 15 years she has been sheltering under the umbrella of the United States nuclear deterrent. I do not believe that it has been wrong to do that. If we are serious in our fight against communism, the choice is not simply nuclear arms or no nuclear arms. It does mean choosing the best weapons which will serve the national policy we have decided upon. Morally speaking, there is little difference between a rifle with a bullet in it and a Bomarc with a nuclear head on it.
In considering the moral aspect in its most extreme form, the nuclear bomb is basically one of mass destruction. This is the H-bomb. This is the bomb carried by the intercontinental ballistic missile, by the heavy bombers which fly overhead, by the Polaris submarines. It is the technique of warfare which brings about mass destruction. It brings the terror of total destruction to force the way of the aggressor upon an unwilling victim. This is the nuclear offensive weapon of mass destruction as carried by the carriers I have outlined.
Let us remember that there are also other weapons of mass destruction. There is bacteriological warfare, poison gas, ray warfare, the poisoning of food and water supplies. Yes, and even conventional arms may come under this classification. I was surprised when in Tokyo the other day to learn that in a number of single bombing raids during the last months of the war more people were killed in Tokyo than in the dropping of the atomic bomb at Hiroshima. I believe that the

Supply-External Affairs use of all such weapons is a crime against humanity and is not justifiable on any moral grounds whatsoever.
It should be made clear too that there are two types of nuclear weapons which do not fall within the category of weapons of indiscriminate or uncontrollable mass destruction. One is the ground-to-air missile of comparatively small range and limited fall-out and used for the purpose of military troops in the field. I believe that such weapons are entirely different from the heavy nuclear bomb of mass destruction. The decision for their adoption must be made on the basis of military advisability. I agree that our forces cannot be "sitting ducks" for an enemy which they face and which has superior weapons to what they have. A few weeks ago I visited the Canadian cemetery in Hong Kong. Here I found the grave markers of many a young Canadian who gave his life in December, 1942 to defend that outpost in world war II. These men were sent to defend Hong Kong ill-equipped, improperly trained, and they became easy prey for an enemy which they did not believe existed. This cannot happen again.
The second type of weapon is the nucleararmed anti-missile missile, examples of which are the Bomarc or the Voodoo aircraft. The aim of such weapon is not to cause destruction of any person or territory but to destroy in flight hostile rockets or aeroplanes carrying these rockets which menace our country or continent. These are defensive weapons particularly as they relate to Canada in our geographic position, because by no means could they reach enemy territory.
Let us now look at the second aspect, namely the economic aspect. From the economic point of view Canada is a nation of limited population and resources placed in the uncomfortable position of being the buffer state between the United States of America and the U.S.S.R. I do not believe that Canada should or even could as a matter of fact, manufacture or obtain her own independent nuclear deterrent. It is significant that while the balance of world power would be small, the danger in extending the scope of the nuclear club would be great. Even Khrushchev has not allowed his satellites to have the nuclear bomb in their hands, not even in Cuba. We would be wise in Canada to respect this unwritten convention for the sake of keeping world tension to a minimum.
We must also consider the military and strategic aspect of this military picture. It is sound policy to say that any government is responsible to see to it that at all times their nation is prepared to defend herself


against any aggressor or any intruder to the best of our physical and economic ability. It is also our responsibility and privilege to share in the collective security which we have without friends, and to fulfil any or all commitments it is necessary to make. However, our big problem now is that we do not know how far our commitments go. We do not know this with regard to NATO. We do not know whether or not we have any specific commitments to NORAD or NATO. Strategically our need goes further than that. We are losing this war against communism because we are not fighting on many fronts where the weapons are not shooting ones, as we know them, but rather weapons of intrigue, subversive propaganda, trade infiltration and economic disruption. We dare not be so smug as to think we can win this cold war using the methods of world war II or of world war I. If we are to develop a peaceful world we must get away from the use of force upon our fellow man. Rather, we must prefer to give him our help, our friendship, our trade. In the first instance, this responsibility extends to the nations who are one with us in the cold war struggle. I believe there are a number of points which more or less sum up this entire picture for us.
I think we should methodically approach these points in an intelligent way with the information we must have in order to do it. I believe our responsibility to our electorate requires this procedure.
First of all, what are the logical policies which develop out of this approach? On behalf of my party I pledge that Social Credit will never adopt or support a defence policy whereby Canada adopts or makes use of offensive weapons of indiscriminate or uncontrollable mass destruction. Canada should indeed use its best efforts to promote the complete abandonment of this type of armament throughout the world, through effectively supervised multilateral international agreement.
The second point concerns whether or not Canada should acquire nuclear defensive weapons at this time at home or with NATO. The leader of the Liberal party has said that we must acquire nuclear armaments in order to keep our commitments with NORAD, with NATO. This is a reversal of the policies he enunciated up until the last couple of weeks.
No.
I wish to ask him what these commitments are. Have we agreed to accept nuclear weapons or have we not done so?
Ask the Prime Minister.
I would ask the government, the Minister of National Defence, the Prime Minister the same question.
And get three different answers.

When we agreed to purchase Bomarcs, did we agree to equip them with nuclear warheads? What about the Star-fighter? What about the Voodoo? Is the question of NATO weaponry a Canadian decision? Is it a bilateral decision or is it a multilateral decision? What is our responsibility to NATO? If it is secret let us say so, and tell the public. After all, that is the only way in which we can be informed. Let me say that this question of emotionalism is no basis upon which to settle the problem before us. How can this house make any sound decision before it has the facts. I say that the onus is on the government to make these necessary facts available. We on our side of the house agree that a special defence committee should be set up. It is absolutely imperative that a means of continued sound approach to the safety of this country be instituted. Let us not forget that consideration. We in Social Credit are convinced that Canada's defence policy must not be a matter of partisan politics or party squabbles.
The Prime Minister so far has refused to set up an all-party parliamentary committee on defence. We believe he is wrong in this refusal. It would be well for him to remember that this is a house of minorities and that neither he nor any of us knows which political party will be responsible for Canada's government and defence policy even three months from now. We ask that all parties together may have a chance to work out with proper information a constructive policy for our country in its relations with other nations of the world and in our own internal policy in which Canadians of every political allegiance can have confidence. The answer to this second point cannot be answered until we have the facts before us and until something of this type has been done. What if we should go into an election in the next week and another Cuban crisis arises during this election period? How could we meet our commitments then? What if there should be a change of government and if in the first few days of that government we should face a crisis? This is something that we collectively in this house of minorities ought to consider if we are to be responsible to the charge that is laid upon us. I believe that the nuclear question has been made far more complicated by the indiscriminate lumping together in the public mind of every variety and form of nuclear armament as if it all were identical. Nuclear weapons of tactical military use, such as the 27507-3-196J
Supply-External Affairs Bomarc, have been lumped together with 24 megaton nuclear bombs as if each would cause equal destruction and each had the same purpose.
By whom?

I am speaking now of the public impression of this matter. It is becoming more and more apparent that no military force can afford to be without such tactical nuclear weapons when opposed by forces which have those weapons. Their deficiency in firepower would be so great that they could not longer be considered to be an effective fighting force. I believe it is ridiculous to use the argument that because the 24 megaton bomb is a bomb of mass destruction, there cannot be defensive weapons which in an emergency are legitimate. It is asking us to throw out the baby with the bath water. Whether such weapons are a defensive military necessity in the defence of our country, or whether we have given a commitment to an ally to adopt such defensive weapons, it is a question which must be answered now and it must be answered by this house. The government has the main responsibility in the matter simply because it is the government. It is the responsibility of this parliament to speak clearly on these points and it is the responsibility of the government to state clear their policy. However, all fit into the world picture to which we are now committed.
I should just like to make one more remark in connection with this second point. Canada for years now has been sheltering under the umbrella of the nuclear deterrent of the United States. For our own good I believe it is our duty and our responsibility to help keep this deterrent strong. I believe that we must assist in maintaining a strong surveillance system, an efficient anti-submarine force in full co-operation with the United States. These are just the facts of our geographic location. We must also equip our three services with sufficient highly mobile, conventional, effectively co-ordinated defence equipment. Such forces must be completely mobile in this day and age, equipped with only the best and most modern equipment. We should discard all land equipment which cannot be air-lifted. Our air force should be equipped with the best tactical aircraft and light and heavy transport. These permanent forces should be supported by strong forces of civilian soldiers and a university training program.

Third, I would say that we must intensify our efforts toward multilateral nuclear disarmament and total military disarmament. We must continue without respite our efforts through the United Nations and by international negotiations to obtain effective international disarmament. The enlargement of the nuclear club and the expansion of the nuclear stockpile must be stopped. Perhaps Mr. Khrushchev removed all the missiles from Cuban soil, but let us remember that just the other day in east Berlin he said that the 60 missiles from Cuba have become 120 missiles elsewhere. We are also told that communist China will have nuclear bombs within the next year or two. Surely civilization will never resort to the destruction of itself. As a pioneer, peace-loving friendly people Canadians can reach their evident place in destiny as champions for a sane, vitally needed armament control program.
At this point it is well to remember that effective disarmament can only come as a result of peace. Peace will never come as a result of disarmament. Disarmament will come as a result of peace. Because if we have no peace there is no chance of reaching a disarmament agreement as we think of it today. Nevertheless we must continue to work for it. Yes, Canada must continue to take part in disarmament negotiations wherever and whenever they might be held. We want to be there when the first crack in the wall appears that might lead us through to something that is definite in this regard. We want to be there when the first ray of light appears through the darkness that now divides the world and makes disarmament impossible. In addition it is our responsibility to make our services available and our influence felt in any armament control agreement that may come in the process of disarmament negotiations, however small it may be. Arms control even through international agreements can never bring about an established peace, though it can and will serve toward lessening the probability and the destructiveness of war and lead us on to the peace that we all agree we should have.
In the fourth place, I would say that on the positive side in our own hemisphere the need for Canada to join the organization of American states is urgent and it has been for many months. Bolivia can never survive without United States financial assistance. Peru may even vote in a communist government next year. The Argentine becomes more and more vulnerable. Venezuela and Guatemala are unstable. Panama threatens to be a hot spot. Cuba has already fallen. Communist
[The Chairman.]
penetration in all these areas is intense. The population of these countries is soaring. It is estimated that within 25 years the population of Latin America will double to more than 400 million people. Desperately they need the material and moral aid we can give from within the O.A.S., which is basically a non-military organization.
In the fifth place, we must turn to the positive role of mutual understanding and help. We will never be far wrong in our defence against communism if we think of those who need our aid as people who, without it, may turn to the communists because the communists tell them that they can do more for them. Communism and the forces of totalitarianism are on the march. We who care for the individual must go on the offensive also, to respect the rights and the desperate needs of the people, particularly those who live in the emerging nations. Can we do this if we are actually cutting back our foreign aid appropriation? This aid involves developing realistic trade and mutual assistance policies with our friends, so that our surpluses that we wish to export will go to them, not to the powers that are seeking to destroy both them and us. We must recognize that in the war which engages the attention of the greatest part of mankind, the war against want, we have been endowed by nature with the most plentiful supply of resources of any country in the world. Surely with these Canada can take a lead towards the development of the world's needy nations. This will prove far better in the long-range objective.
The sixth point I wish to bring to the attention of the house involves Canada's trade policies. They must be co-ordinated with her external affairs policies. Since one third of all jobs in Canada depend on exports, it is assumed that every sale we make abroad is beneficial to our economy and consequently to the well-being of the nation. This type of trade thinking is completely divorced from political considerations that might be involved. We simply trade with anyone who has the necessary cash or credit. This is in line with the old English principle and tradition which regards trade as a non-political activity and bars trade only with the enemy in wartime. Such an approach to world trade would be justified if all our trading partners regarded it in the same light. Unfortunately in the east-west conflict which has developed a whole scale of new methods of warfare trade is regarded and used by our adversary as a major weapon.
If we accept the premise that we are at war with the communists and that this war is being waged almost exclusively by nonmilitary means, then we must change our

concept of international trade. Whether we like it or not we must accept the fact that trade has become an integral and perhaps the basic and most important part of our struggle for the survival of freedom. Once we grasp this fact it should not be difficult to recognize the suicidal nature of our present trade policy. This does not only apply to the so-called strategic materials. Simply because the communists openly declare and emphatically pursue a policy which is intended to destroy our social system, when we strengthen them we are increasing their chances of reaching their goal.
The difficulty in recognizing the danger in trading with the communist bloc lies in the temporary material benefits which our economy derives from such trade. It is virtually impossible to persuade a manufacturer or an exporter or a farmer, shall we say, that trade with communist countries is in the long run suicidal. It is equally difficult for the government to recognize the danger when every increase in exports, regardless of where they go, helps to create jobs and stimulate domestic economic activity. Since employment and domestic activity are the main pillars of political and financial stability, every government in the free world and every government in the communist world as well is extremely reluctant to let consideration of the harsh realities enter into the trade picture, just as we are in setting up our pattern of foreign trade.
Individual and collective greed, whether we like to admit it or not, is the motivating power of the economies of the democratic countries and it makes it virtually impossible for the governments of these countries to correlate trade with foreign defence policies.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
Would he agree that hunger is the greatest threat to peace today?

I agree, and I would add that the greatest threat to peace as it relates to hunger lies in those countries that are still on the western side of this cold war and who would like to remain there. Just remember that hungry bellies do not care about votes and do not care about democracy. They need to have their wants satisfied.
What about full bellies?

I would say that if what you are referring to in your question actually reached the objective which you are thinking of then there might be more reason for your question, but I happen to know that the biggest part of it is not.
Supply-External Affairs
How do you know?

It is quite an easy fact to understand. Come along with me to the Far East and we will certainly find out for ourselves a lot more than you know at this time. Yet, I would say this; without such correlation we can never hope to fight effectively this strange new war that is being forced upon us by international communism. We will, in fact, trade ourselves into defeat and slavery. Moscow and Peking can at any time plunge us into serious economic difficulty, yes and political difficulty too; just remember that on the other side of the house. They can do this by suddenly stopping our exports and at the same time undercutting our prices, by flooding world markets with some of their own raw materials and products.
This may not happen tomorrow. It may not happen next year. But it is bound to happen eventually. The communists are not using trade for profit as we are. They are using trade for the mutual benefit of the participants as political weapons. At this stage of the global conflict they are agreeing to trade with us, to take as much of our exports as they can pay for or promise to pay for, because our flow of goods helps to build up their strength rapidly, even as it did for Hitler in the prewar years and also because it sucks us into dependency upon them.
It is a crying indictment of our policies that we are so blinded by the profit motive or by political expediency, for example, that we are digging our own graves. Our weak and insipid foreign, defence and trade policies are the direct result of our ideological blindness. This folly is neither new nor typically Canadian. It is characteristic of the inability of the west as a whole to comprehend the nature of the global struggle with communism in this cold war. It is also characteristic of our inability to comprehend that, in order to survive in this conflict, we cannot afford to put business interests before political and defence considerations.
Now, the issue would be clear if we were at war in the traditional way with the communist countries. We would then most certainly not trade with the enemy, just as we did not trade with the axis powers during the second world war. No amount of money would have induced us to ship grain or anything else to nazi Germany, Italy or Japan while the fighting was taking place. But has the picture changed at this point in the very basic issues? I do not think it has. The trouble, then, stems from the lack of realization that there is a direct conflict involving Canada. We are in every other sense at war with militant communism which makes no bones about its desire to destroy our political, economic and social structure. By permitting almost the total amount of our present trade expansion

Supply-External Affairs to develop with communist countries, be it tor monetary gain or for reasons of domestic political expediency, we are helping them to accomplish their aim. There is nothing to beat such a policy for suicidal stupidity.
Now, just as defence, trade is an extension of foreign policy. To change our foreign trade we must, therefore, change our foreign policy. Any meaningful revision of our economic thinking must therefore start with a thorough examination of our role in the cold war. This whole issue we are talking about right now is more critical at this point than the question of nuclear arms. After the shocks of the Cuban emergency and the Chinese invasion of India, such a reappraisal can no longer be postponed. Since our national economy is deeply involved in the process, this debate is the logical place to start such a reappraisal. This is a debate of our defence policy, our foreign affairs policy, and I maintain interrelated with them is our trade policy.
Now, to be reasonable about this problem, we cannot cut off immediately or drastically reduce our trade with communist countries. This would undoubtedly have adverse effects on our economy. How can we minimize and gradually eliminate the harmful effects of the political impelling force in our foreign trade? This can be done basically by reorienting our trade to the areas of the free world. It might entail a complete revision of our commonwealth trade policies. The commonwealth is the logical place to begin such a reorientation. I maintain that at this particular time when Britain is having problems in joining the European common market, that this is the logical time to call for a commonwealth trade conference, and to call for it soon. I have said this before, and I believe the need is greater and the opportunity is greater at this point than it has been at any time in the last six months.
It is inevitable to the survival of Canada that ultimately we will have common market arrangements with the United States within a reasonable number of years. Let us take the initiative now in seriously exploring that proposition. Why do we wait? Why are we indecisive? Are we not able to grasp the things that are involved?
There is a tremendous opportunity for increased trade in the Caribbean area which is now waiting for action, not words, to quote a newspaper article in one of the Ottawa newspapers last night. The entire American hemisphere will eventually provide a better outlet for our exports than all of the trade we could ever develop with communist countries, with the great population and the tremendous market potential it has. In this regard, it is interesting to note that just last week Soviet Russia worked out a deal to expand her

wheat trade with Brazil. In fact, the expected trade increase with Brazil is going to be 50 per cent greater this next year than it was last year.
What about the cold war? We can go on and on talking about these opportunities that we have, but we must consider them in their full light. I would say that in addition there is a seventh point that is very important. I refer to our own financial and economic position. We all agree that per capita Canada is one of the richest nations in the world. We all agree that while we have a high standard of living, our financial and economic system has not permitted the expansion that should have developed. We can never survive in Canada with 18 million people. I notice that Japan is intending to double its gross national product in the next ten years. I believe that this is something we can do, too. Our population can be increased by 50 per cent in the same period. It is because of the defects in their economic systems that the governments of the rich nations of the world have come to rely more and more on the production of instruments of war which do not have to be sold in any market place to distribute income and provide employment for their workers. This was the method used by the axis powers prior to the beginning of world war II.
I am frightened that this very same economic technique of the placing of armament contracts to promote full employment has even become evident in our own policies in Canada. It is apparent in the United States also, that they are using the machinery of an expanded arms and space program financed through deficit financing, to keep the nation's economy in a state of buoyancy. It is idle for us to expect permanent peace in the world when the pressures of our economic system, enhance the possibility of a profitable contract to the armaments manufacturers, when employment and the means of life for great numbers of workers-directly or indirectly- demand the continuation of the arms race to prevent an uncontrollable recession. If we seek the long term lessening of world tensions, it is time that we studied very closely the workings of our capitalist economy, and the economies of the countries in the free world, to find out by what paradox it is that when we prepare ourselves for the very wasteful destructiveness of war, we become rich instead of poor.
This is one of the reasons that during the years of the Liberal administration from 1945, shall we say, to 1955, we had prosperity. It was simply because we were living off all the prosperity that developed as a result of world war II. Therefore I think it is high

time we in Canada looked at this thing in the over-all perspective in order that we face up to the responsibilities that are before us. Thus I believe the debate in which we are taking part is at the right time and is the ideal place for us to begin a real, soul-searching look into the problems we face in our relationships with the rest of the world.
So far as external affairs are concerned we cannot separate defence policies or trade policies. I believe of all people in the world we, because of our heritage, because of who and what we are, are standing on the threshold of a new era of greatest expansion and development for the human race. I say let us take a lead in it, if only we have the courage, conviction, determination and will to move forward. This is the responsibility I see before us.
Will my hon. friend permit a question?
Yes.
Will my hon. friend say if his party believes that the Canadian government should fulfil the commitments it has to NATO and NORAD?
I would like to know what those commitments are.
Ask your friend.

I believe there is a grave responsibility on the government to tell us what they are, and if they are secret it should say so. If they are something which should not be brought out in public, then let us form a non-partisan defence committee where these things can be brought out in a nonpolitical atmosphere such as we have not had during the last 12 months or so.

Mr. Chairman, this debate on external affairs and defence estimates is long overdue. This parliament began its sittings on September 27, and it seems to me a shameful thing that in all these weeks and months we have not yet had any clearcut statement from the government regarding its policy on nuclear weapons, and that this is the first opportunity we have had in the house to debate Canada's role in international affairs.
In the next few weeks and months this country will be faced with fateful and far reaching decisions, particularly with reference to nuclear weapons, and it seems to me imperative that the people of Canada should know where the various political parties stand so that the people can make a decision as to what course this country should follow in the interests of maintaining peace and security throughout the world.

I must say, Mr. Chairman, that I was disappointed this afternoon with the statements made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the international spokesman for the Liberal party, the hon. member for Essex East. International affairs, defence, and the whole question of nuclear weapons are irretrievably bound up together. The minister made no statement regarding the government's policy on nuclear weapons. Of course I may say he interrupted his speech. I believe he is going to resume it, and it may be that later on in the course of his speech he will make reference to this matter but certainly, in so far as his resume this afternoon of the international situation was concerned, there might have been no such thing as a problem of nuclear armament. The same is true, of course, of the speech made by the hon. member for Essex East.
I would like to say in great kindness to both hon. members, for both of whom I have very high regard, that the people of Canada are not concerned with whether it was a Liberal government or a Conservative government that first protested in the United Nations against Soviet imperialism. We expect our governments to take that position.
What the people of Canada want to know is what policy is this country going to follow, what commitments have been made, why have they been made, to what extent are they going to be implemented, what does it mean in terms of Canada's future and what does it mean for the peace of the world.
We in the New Democratic party believe that the No. 1 issue facing the world today is how can we prevent a nuclear war. For the first time in his long history man has it within his power to destroy himself. Throughout the centuries we have fought wars that have killed people in their thousands. Two recent wars killed people in their millions, but when the first atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki a new age was born. Mankind has slowly awakened to the fact that man now has within his hand the power to destroy civilization and even life on this planet. It is estimated that the United States and the Soviet union between them have stockpiled sufficient nuclear missiles to have the explosive equivalent of 50 tons of t.n.t. for every man, woman and child on the face of the earth, and when military men speak of the need for a nuclear deterrent surely there can be no gainsaying the fact that we have such a deterrent, a deterrent of terrifying magnitude.
We in this party believe that all Canada's energies should be directed towards preventing a nuclear holocaust, and to lose sight of

Supply-External Affairs that fact in the intricacies of discussing military estimates could be disastrous. This basic fact should be the cornerstone of our foreign policy and all our decisions, all our programs, expenditures and energies should be founded on the determination to contribute to man's desperate quest for peace.
The second thing the New Democratic party sets forth is that we believe that the No. 2 problem is to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons. The world's best hope lies in persuading the two great nuclear powers, the United States and the Soviet union, to reach some agreement fast regarding the cessation of nuclear tests, both for the sake of the health of the millions of people now living as well as for future human survival. Second, to negotiate a treaty for nuclear disarmament under international inspection and control. Everyone knows that will not be an easy task, but in recent days there have been some signs that give reason for hope and optimism. We maintain that the proliferation of nuclear weapons will make this task more difficult, if not impossible. Reaching some viable agreement between the two major nuclear powers has proven long and difficult, but every addition to the world nuclear club will only compound and multiply that difficulty.
We maintain that Canada's best contribution to the peace of the world consists In refusing to acquire nuclear weapons for Canada's forces either at home or abroad. For Canada to become a nuclear power, no matter under what pretext, is to invite the growth of the world's nuclear club. If Canada accepts nuclear weapons from the United States, that country will be under pressure to make the same weapons available to its friends in Europe and in Asia, and eventually in Africa. In turn the Soviet union will be under pressure from its friends to supply nuclear weapons to the countries with which it is allied. Every addition to the nuclear club increases by geometric progression the danger that some irresponsible megalomaniac will press the button and precipitate the world into a nuclear holocaust. It is difficult enough to persuade the two major powers to reach some acceptable agreement for nuclear disarmament. How much greater-nay, impossible-will be the task when 15 or 20 nations have a nuclear capacity at their disposal.
While we all hope that there will be no outbreak in Europe, we must remember that this is always a possibility. If that unfortunate eventuality should take place, then it is imperative that we contain it. The use of nuclear tactical weapons would make this virtually impossible, because it would lead automatically to the full scale use of strategical nuclear weapons. Almost every military

authority in the world-in the western world at least-has now abandoned the theory of limited nuclear tactical warfare.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to just look for a moment at the policy which the government has followed in respect of this question. In my opinion the government has never been either frank or fair with the people of Canada. Apparently they made commitments in 1959 to acquire nuclear weapons which they knew would be worthless without nuclear warheads. They were either wasting public funds or they intended to acquire nuclear warheads for the Bomarcs, the Voodoo planes, the Honest John rocket artillery and the CF-104's. Instead of telling the people frankly that they intended to acquire nuclear weapons, they played this game of, "Now you see it; now you don't".
The Minister of National Defence and his public relations staff have ground out propaganda telling the Canadian people that our military forces simply cannot carry on without nuclear weapons. At the same time the Secretary of State for External Affairs has gone about making excellent speeches giving reasons why we should not acquire nuclear weapons. This has been a government with two voices. While I am not questioning the sincerity' of either minister, I would say that after listening to them it was always difficult to believe that they sat in the same cabinet or that they were members of the same government. If they do not intend to acquire nuclear weapons, we should know why they are continuing this inexcusable waste of public funds. I am told that only a few of the CF-104's, or Starfighters, as they are called, have thus far been delivered, but I understand that the government has contracted for the acceptance of 200 in all. Without nuclear warheads, General Norstad says, these have little military value, yet we keep on spending money despite changing military concepts that make nuclear strike 'planes less valuable. If the Skybolt, which the British are now planning to discard, is nearing obsolescence, it would seem that this would be even more true of the CF-104. We have a long list of 'planes, such as the Vampire, the Starjet, the CF-100, and the ill-fated Arrow, on which the Canadian government over the years have spent hundreds of millions of dollars of the taxpayers money.
I say that the government's policy on the question of nuclear arms has been one of indecision and timidity. They have followed the policy of "nuclear arms if necessary, but not necessarily nuclear arms", which has a familiar ring in Canadian political history. They have never yet, however, defined what is meant by the word "necessary". I assume

that probably the public relations experts, past and present, will watch the Gallup poll and decide when they become "necessary".
I urge the government to come out from behind this smokescreen of double-talk and take a stand. I say to the government: If you have made a mistake in giving commitments, then be honest and renegotiate those commitments both in NATO and in NORAD. The Canadian people will forgive you if you have made an honest error in judgment. But they will not forgive you if you make a transparent attempt to deceive them by refusing nuclear arms with one hand and buying them with the other.
I agree with the fine tribute which the Secretary of State for External Affairs paid this afternoon to Canada's contribution on the disarmament committee of 18 and to the splendid work which has been done by General Burns. If we have followed closely the deliberations of that committee I am sure we have all been proud of the extent to which the representatives of the eight non-aligned nations have looked to Canada in many instances to speak on their behalf. I think this is one of the finest tributes that has ever been paid to Canadian integrity and Canadian diplomacy. But I want to say to the minister that the moral influence which Canada now exerts in the disarmament committee will be very seriously impaired the day Canada becomes a member of the nuclear club. It is well to remember Emerson's words, "What you are speaks so loudly I can't hear what you say".
May I make just a passing reference, Mr. Chairman, to the position of the Liberal party on this question of nuclear arms. The leader of the Liberal party has now committed his party to the acquiring of nuclear arms, and did so in a speech on January 12 at York-Scarborough Liberal convention. The talk of negotiating out afterwards was, in my opinion, just a sedative for the more disturbed members of the party who were protesting. This new Liberal policy was made without consultation with the membership of that party and represents a complete about-face from the position which the Liberal party took prior to the last general election.
At a Liberal rally in the city of Ottawa-

Mr. Chairman, before I was interrupted I was in the process of quoting the leader of the Liberal party in a statement he made at a Liberal rally in the city of Ottawa in January, 1961. The press quotes him as saying:
We should not acquire nuclear weapons under any kind ol national or joint control.
The Toronto Star of November 10, 1962 says as follows:
Canada should renegotiate her commitments with NATO to take a non-nuclear role in the western alliance. Liberal Lester B. Pearson said yesterday. He told the Canadian committee for nuclear disarmament that Canada could negotiate for a nonnuclear role in NATO and still fulfil all her obligations to that alliance.
So I am saying that the position now taken by the Liberal party is a complete about-face. Every party, of course, has a right to make an about-face, but I am simply putting on the record that this is the case.
It is not the first time though.

I want to point out that the Liberal position is completely without logic when they say, in effect "We do not want nuclear weapons, but since we are committed to accept them then we should take them and then try to renegotiate ourselves out of them". Why not negotiate ourselves out now? What, in effect, the leader of the Liberal party is saying is that we should sign a bilateral agreement. We should train personnel in the use of nuclear weapons, knowing all the time we are doing so that we are going to renegotiate ourselves out the moment the ink is dry on the paper.
Isn't that terrible.
It is stupid.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: It is Liberal.

Neither the leader of the Liberal party nor anybody else has given us any convincing reason why having these nuclear weapons would favour the cause of peace. On the contrary, all the arguments

Supply-External Affairs given by the Leader of the Opposition in his speech at the York-Scarborough convention lead logically to the opposite conclusion. Really the only reason he gave why Canada should accept nuclear weapons was because we were committed to accept them. Does this apply to all the other commitments made by a Conservative government? If it did, then there is little use in the Leader of the Opposition's trying to change the government. The President of the United States, President Kennedy, did not hesitate to renegotiate the agreement with Great Britain on the Skybolt when he thought this would be beneficial.
Acceptance of nuclear weapons by Canada is not a condition of our membership in NATO, as is evidenced by the fact that Denmark and Norway and some other countries have not accepted nuclear weapons. Rather than nuclear weapons giving us greater security, the evidence is all the other way. The United States nuclear deterrent is estimated to be five times as great as that of the Soviet union. Even Great Britain's tremendous expenditure on nuclear weapons has given her only 2 per cent of the west's nuclear deterrent. Canada's contribution, therefore, to the west's deterrent would be insignificant militarily, but it would do tremendous harm in proliferating the acquisition of nuclear arms and would therefore far offset any military value which might accrue.
I am sure many hon. members are familiar with Henry A. Kissinger, who has for many years been the chief proponent in the United States of the use of nuclear arms and nuclear strategy. It is rather interesting that in the July 1962 issue of Foreign Affairs he has written an article on this question. I shall ask the committee to bear with me while I read just a very short excerpt from it. Mr. Kissinger said:
The present deployment of NATO's nuclear capability represents an anomaly in terms of current NATO doctrine. Nuclear weapons and delivery systems for technical use have been placed in Europe in considerable numbers. Yet deputy secretary of defense Gilpatric has rejected the notion of tactical nuclear war.
Then he quotes Gilpatric as saying:
"I, for one, have never believed in a so-called limited nuclear war. 1 just don't know how you build a limit into it once you start using any kind of a nuclear bang".
Then Kissinger goes on:
And this view seems to have been reinforced by secretary McNamara at the NATO ministerial meeting in Athens.
At the same time, secretary McNamara has insisted that in case of general war our strategic forces are alone sufficient to perform any nuclear mission.
Then he quotes McNamara as saying:
"There is no question but today our strategic retaliatory forces of bombers, missiles and Polaris


are fully capable of destroying Soviet targets, even after absorbing an initial nuclear surprise attack".
Kissinger winds up this part of his argument by saying this:
In these terms, the nuclear establishment on the continent is both dangerous and useless. It is dangerous because it may make inevitable the limited nuclear war both Mr. McNamara and Mr. Gilpatric have declared is certain to escalate. And it is useless because it will merely duplicate attacks on targets already covered by our strategic forces.
Therefore the whole idea, which I understood the hon. member for Red Deer to expound, that you can make a differentiation between tactical nuclear weapons and strategic nuclear weapons, and that you can have a limited tactical nuclear war, has now been abandoned by nearly all of the military experts today, men like Kissinger, John Stra-chey, the former secretary for war in the British government, John Gellner, and many others.
We believe that Canada should not accept nuclear weapons. We believe that as far as NORAD is concerned this was designed to meet the threat of attacks from manned bombers. But today manned bombers are no longer the real threat. Intercontinental ballistic missiles and nuclear missiles from submarines are the growing danger. Against these there is no defence other than the threat of the massive deterrent. We believe that the warning systems should be retained as long as they have any value but that nuclear warheads for Bomarcs have no military value and would lessen Canada's position in promoting nuclear containment.
In so far as NATO is concerned, we note that even the United States authorities are veering away from stressing the value of nuclear tactical weapons. These were thought of in the first instance as a means of gaining time during the period when the Soviet union had a preponderance in conventional forces;
I refer to gaining time until the United States could build up its technical and strategic nuclear arsenal. As the Secretary of State for External Affairs pointed out this afternoon, that arsenal is now so great that the United States has a tremendous preponderance. It is significant that the nuclear missile bases in both Italy and Turkey are being dismantled and that the real defence now will be the use of the I.C.B.M. missiles and the Polaris submarine.
The two great dangers of tactical nuclear weapons in the hands of NATO forces is summed up in the two terms now used by the military, namely escalation and proliferation. As to escalation, the military authorities recognize that the concept of a limited nuclear action is no longer accepted. They recognize

the fact that kilotons on the Elbe would mean, in a matter of days or hours, megatons on the Volga and on the Hudson. This is why President Kennedy has been stressing the fact that conventional forces should have increasing importance in NATO and that the use of conventional forces would provide a "pause" during which it might be possible to contain the conflict before resorting to the ultimate strategic nuclear deterrent.
The other danger is the danger of proliferation.
