Mr. Chairman, I thank hon. members for their indulgence. I can assure them that I will try not to impose on their generosity.
Even military authorities are becoming increasingly concerned about the difficulty in controlling tactical nuclear weapons when they get into the hands of a number of nations. The Nassau declaration is the outcome of a struggle between, on the one hand, the United States which desires to keep control of the nuclear deterrent, and on the other hand, certain European leaders who are recklessly pressing for independent nuclear capacity, not for military reasons but in order to bolster an outmoded concept of national prestige.
I have serious doubts about the safety of having 15 fingers on one trigger, but I have no doubt about the fact that 15 fingers on 15 separate triggers would mean disaster for mankind. We in the New Democratic party believe that any proliferation, whether to independent nations or to NATO as a multinational nuclear power, would add immeasurably to the danger of nuclear war and should be resisted.
We in this party believe that Canada should have a positive program for peace consistent with the type of contribution which we can best make toward establishing collective security in the world. Canada cannot divorce itself from the world in which it lives. Canada's foreign policy should not be a neutralist one. The program of the New Democratic party drafted here in the city of Ottawa in our founding convention stated as follows:
In the struggle between democracy and totalitarianism, Canada cannot evade its responsibility;
Supply-External Affairs
it must always stand squarely on the side of freedom and with the genuine forces of freedom.
Our policy cannot be one of pacifism. A refusal to fight is no guarantee of immunity from attack. In the world community, just as in the local community, there will always be those who, from a desire for personal gain or a lust for power, will resort to banditry. The present dispute between India and China is a glaring example of the fact that even an unprovocative nation is not free from aggression.
Canada's policy, it seems to me, would be unrealistic if we were to advocate unilateral nuclear disarmament. In the present nuclear stalemate it is merely wishful thinking to suggest that either of the great nuclear powers should discard their nuclear weapons unless they can be assured of an effective system of inspection and control under which they will be guaranteed that while they are disarming, the other party to the agreement is doing likewise.
Canada's role should be to work for a system of collective security under the United Nations. Regional alliances must never be regarded as a substitute, and even when they are necessary they must be considered as a temporary expedient pending the development of a world authority clothed with the necessary power to keep the peace. This situation cannot be brought about overnight and cannot be whistled up out of nothing. It will involve using all our influence to strengthen the United Nations in its various activities. For years public men have talked about establishing a permanent international police force. Yet after 18 years we have not yet attained this objective.
The United Nations has had more success in putting out "brush fires" than many of its detractors had anticipated. Suez, the Egyptian-Israeli war, the present conflict in the Congo and the Cuban episode all gave evidence of the fact that, when solidly backed by world opinion, it is possible for the United Nations to take police action to stop the spread of military conflict. I would draw the attention of the committee, however, to the fact that these police actions have been taken with conventional military forces and it is here that Canada could play its most effective role by offering to make its military forces and equipment ready and available for a permanent international police force.
Canada should use its influence to remove some of the tensions that are likely to provoke military conflict. We should seek military disengagement in central Europe along much the same line as that followed in the case of Austria. We must seek a solution to the Berlin situation and the eventual

Supply-External Affairs signing of a German peace treaty. It is 18 years since the war ended and until some agreement is reached Berlin will continue to be a powder keg that can explode at any minute. Canada should make it clear that we will work for the right of self-determination for all peoples but that we are not prepared to lend ourselves to military adventures to satisfy the illusions of grandeur which seem to have taken hold of some of our allies in recent months and years.
In conclusion I want to say that Canada can make a much greater contribution to the positive programs for peace that are so urgently needed throughout the world. Today we are spending about $1J billion per year on defence, much of it for equipment which is already obsolete, but we are contributing less than one twentieth of that amount for programs like the Colombo plan and in providing help for underprivileged and underdeveloped countries. Canada is not a great power in military terms or in the size of our population. Our military contribution is relatively unimportant in the sum total of military forces as they exist in the world today, but in terms of economic aid Canada can play a role out of all proportion to its population and size.
Food is one of the most important weapons in the arsenal of democracy. The New Democratic party at its founding convention endorsed the idea of having Canada contribute 2 per cent of its gross national product to assist underdeveloped areas. This would mean an expenditure of $700 million to $800 million a year to provide food, consumer and capital goods, medical supplies and technical personnel, which in our opinion would do more in the long run to remove the causes of war and to promote peace than the purchase of a few atomic weapons which would simply be added to an already dangerously large military stockpile.
The 17-man committee of economists which the United Nations appointed to look into the economic problems arising out of disarmament have made an interesting report. They state that all the nations of the world for which statistics are available, are now spending $120 billion a year on defence and are employing 50 million people in their armed services and defence industries. They estimate that if we could turn this money and manpower to peaceful uses we could raise the living standards of the people in every part of the world. We could banish hunger, disease and ignorance. It is in this war against man's age old enemies that Canada can play her most effective role.
I believe that the people of Canada would respond to such a challenge. I am sure there are thousands of young Canadians who would [Mr. Douglas.!

gladly enrol in a Canadian youth service as teachers, nurses, doctors, social workers, engineers and scientists to represent Canada in helping to raise living standards and improve living conditions of people in the underdeveloped areas of the world.
This afternoon the Secretary of State for External Affairs said that there is a longing for peace in the world. I believe he is right. I believe that in every country of the world the people are tired of war and they are tired of living in a balance of terror with the threat of the nuclear bomb hanging over their heads. I believe that in many ways the people of the world are ahead of the statesmen of the world in their anxiety for peace. I believe that the Canadian people are waiting for the government and for this parliament to give a lead to show them how we may work together to promote peace in the world. I submit that this country is waiting to see whether or not we are capable of giving that leadership and whether or not we have the capacity to match the greatness of the times in which we live.
May I ask the hon. member whether he is prepared to tell the house if he is or is not in favour of Canada remaining in NORAD and NATO?

Mr. Chairman, I think I answered the first question. I think that Canada should terminate its agreement under NORAD in so far as supplying Bomarc missiles and Voodoo interceptor planes is concerned, because they no longer have any function in a military sense, and that we should stay in that agreement in so far as supplying warning systems is concerned as long as they have any value. With reference to NATO, I believe we should stay in NATO. I believe that NATO has a function to perform until such time as the United Nations is strong enough to give us the collective security which the world so greatly needs. But I point out that membership in NATO is not conditional upon our accepting nuclear weapons, and that we have a conventional role which we can play in NATO and in the United Nations.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have now had the volleys from the heavy artillery on all sides of the field and I will introduce something of a lighter calibre. The discussion has been a very interesting one so far. I always enjoy hearing from my good friend, the member for Essex East. We have had some good times together. I have a high regard for his ideas, except when he talks about partisan politics, and the only thing that worries me is that he has such a proclivity for talking about partisan politics.

I was interested too in the statements of the other preceding speakers. I think the hon. member for Red Deer is right, of course, when he injects what we must in a country like this always inject, the question of morality in the whole field of international politics as indeed in national politics. There were times, however, when I thought that perhaps the hon. member for Essex East injected partisanship a little too deeply, sharply and unnecessarily. I quite agree with him that Canada has in general looked upon the field of external affairs with a bipartisan approach, although I suppose out of respect to other parties I should say a multipartisan approach. When I was a student and should have been studying I had the opportunity to sit in the gallery of the house and hear external affairs discussions when the hon. gentleman's party was in power in those unhappy days behind us, and I remember that generally there was a transcending of partisanship. I deplore the fact that he discussed in somewhat critical and perhaps cynical terms the position of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. At one time, he invoked indecision, and I thought at the time that was a very dangerous subject for a man in his party which has been noted for its gyrations and inauguration of changes in policy over the past few months.
He did refer to the minister's interview on television, and I looked up the transcript after the hon. member referred to it. I noted that in the very opening statement, the minister said this:
Canada always has stood by her friends, and of course Americans are our friends and we are standing by them.
On the same page of the transcript in answer to another question, the minister said:
We are friends of the United States and we are standing beside them.
This, I think, was an explicit and definite statement. I listened to that interview and I remember, I think we all remember, that was a grave night indeed, the night of October 22. When the minister was asked if he would spell out the gravity of the situation, and he was asked these questions:
Should we start putting watercans in our basement?
Should we start making plans to get out of town?
If this minister, in possession of confidential communications from governments all over the world, had at that time said anything to augment or increase panic in the country, I should think he would not be properly discharging the duties of the high office which he holds.
My hon. friend mentioned another subject on which he and I share views, that is the membership in the organization of American
Supply-External Affairs states. I may say that when his party was in power I was enthused about that and I wondered to myself time and time again why he had not seen that action was taken along those lines. I know and he knows that this government has brought us closer to that very important Latin American world than his government ever did. We are today represented in every single state in Latin America. We have attended inter-American conferences. We have developed contacts with these people which are extremely valuable. I quite agree with the hon. member for Red Deer that the people of Latin America and these important nations to the south with their great problems, their great prospects and possibilities, are worthy of the utmost consideration.
I heard a great international statesman say not long ago that the problems of today which would become most important tomorrow in their development and fulfilment lie with those people below the equator, and the Latin American area is a very important part of that particular set of problems.
I think, too, it was a bit unfair to suggest that the minister had overstated his optimism in the field of disarmament. He has not, through his long political career and his highly successful diplomatic career, been given to overstatement. He has not gone in for excessive optimism. Like the President of the United States, he pointed out today that these strains which may appear within the communist world are not fractures. We all know that the disagreement which interests us would appear to be a disagreement over means and not ends. As the president, that great statesman, said the other day, a dispute over how best to bury the free world is no cause for western rejoicing.
I would say, too, that while the minister during his career has not been noted for excessive optimism he has not been noted for excessive pessimism either. World statesmen have time after time paid tribute to the tenacity with which he held to hope for disarmament. We all pray and hope that these hopes will be realized. He does not, I am sure, claim it alone nor does Canada claim it alone, but down through the course of these difficult and trying negotiations there has been one constant thing and that has been the unyielding determination of Canada to say we shall not give up; we will continue with this great world problem.
There are many aspects of Canadian foreign policy, Mr. Chairman, which are worthy of reflection by this house. In the time at my disposal this evening, I should like to discuss one of those which is very close to my heart and which I believe is becoming more and more meaningful to the people of Canada. I refer to the United Nations and our membership

Supply-External Affairs and role therein. I have had the honour of representing Canada at four general assemblies of the United Nations. This past session, just concluded, struck me as one of the most constructive of these important international gatherings. It seemed that there was a diminution of tension, and lessening of power politics which sometimes makes difficult the day to day progress which is such an important part of an organization which endeavours to make progress on so many fronts.
I believe that in Canada the strain of cynicism is disappearing. We have had people, publicists and others, who believed the United Nations was more a talk shop, that nothing was accomplished, that there was a great disparity in power among the members, that there was not sufficient realism in its construction. I believe the accomplishments of the United Nations in recent years, and they have been enumerated by preceding speakers, have convinced Canadians and others that this great body is in truth the hope of the world as the idealists always said it was. The past session has seen the coming to fruition of a number of projects which had seemed to be discouraging.
One thing which caused great rejoicing, I think, was the confirmation of the secretary general in his office. This great Asian statesman has done a splendid job in one of the most sensitive and difficult posts which the world could convey upon any mortal man. Canada said, from the very beginning, that we were strongly in favour of U Thant's confirmation as secretary general. The minister has referred to the success of the Congo operation and Canada's role in the advisory committee of the United Nations.
I was in the United Nations at the time of the confrontation between Mr. Zorin and Mr. Stevenson, an unforgettable moment of great tension. As has been pointed out, and something which should not be forgotten, the spokesmen for these great super powers, with their tremendous power in comparison to the other members of the United Nations, took that dispute to the very forum of world opinion, the security council. As they faced one another every seat in the security council chamber was filled with members from the general assembly. It was an unforgettable moment. The role of the acting secretary general, as he then was, was highly creditable and crowned with much success.
We are pleased too, that under the inspiration of former president Mongi Slim, the United Nations is moving forward in the direction of improving its procedures and manner of work. A very impressive com-
[Mr. Macquarrie.l
mittee has been set up for which I think lovers of the United Nations may entertain high hopes.
The United Nations, which began with some 50 members, has now 110. The area of the world unrepresented in the U.N. is shrinking daily. Its complexion is changing. Membership of the committees and other bodies is altering and it is necessary in the interests of efficiency to have some improvements in techniques. Indeed it is almost necessary to have an extension to the very physical facilities. These, which once seemed to be so ample, now often appear to be overcrowded.
Mr. Chairman, we in the context of this debate are of course interested in the performance of the Canadian delegation at the United Nations. I was very proud of the way the Canadian delegation performed. There is something extremely humbling to be at an international organization and note on every hand the high respect in which Canadians are held. I think it is humbling because it is quite a challenge to measure up to the tremendous responsibilities constantly put upon Canadians, especially in the U.N. context. We are a charter member of the U.N. I suppose, if one looked back over the whole history of resolutions, Canadians have been co-sponsors or sponsors of more resolutions than any other country.
The Canadian point of view is constantly sought. We have served on all sorts of peace making missions and I think it could be said that this very day Canadian personnel are performing peace keeping operations all over the world. It is something which should cause us pride. At the same time it should cause us some humility because it is a heavy challenge.
Canada took a great many initiatives in the last assembly. One of these dealt with the question discussed by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam just a moment ago. The world food program became fully operational on January 1 of this year. As is known, Canada has taken an active part in the establishment and development of this program, beginning with the Prime Minister's proposal to the United Nations general assembly in September, 1960.
This program will provide assistance by means of foodstuffs in three major fields. It will meet emergency food needs and emergencies arising from chronic malnutrition. It will give assistance in pre-school areas and implement pilot projects, using food as an aid to economic and social development.
Since the idea for a world food program was launched events have moved swiftly. In the last few months a pledging conference has been held at which approximately $88

million in commodities, cash and services were pledged. Canada's pledge totalled $5 million in commodities and cash. An intergovernmental committee, of which Canada is a member, has now been established and has prepared a work program. This, I may say, putting it very simply, is one of the concrete moves in the direction of a better world.
Canada also played a major role in the very serious question of radiation. We would be ill-advised to become so sophisticated that we lost our concern and indeed our fear of what is happening to the atmosphere. Canada moved, and was supported magnificently by the other members of the general assembly, to set up a world organization for the dissemination of information on the harmful effects of radiation and to galvanize world opinion regarding those harmful effects.
I mention some of these things because the hon. member for Essex East was asking about new steps. Canada's initiative in the second committee dealing with international economic relations, and in the conference on world trade development, was a most impressive and most successful one, and great credit is due to Senator Blois who was our representative there, a worthy maritimer who naturally did a most excellent job. There were many, many days when differences were quite acute as to when the conference should be held, how it would be held and who should be involved, but these serious differences have been ironed out and it is now set that the meeting will be held not later than 1964.
The Canadian hope is that after careful preparation the conference will achieve positive proposals for the expansion of trade, particularly by the developing countries, and on December 20 Canada was elected a member of the preparatory committee which will begin its meetings in January. Once again this country, which some would have us believe is ill regarded in the international community, was chosen to take part in the planning of this important job.
Another problem which has been facing the United Nations for some time and is becoming increasingly acute is the very mundane problem of finances and how to keep the organization solvent. In this field through the fifth committee the Canadian delegation was extremely active and I am glad to say extremely successful. We called for an appeal to the international court in respect to the question of members' obligations regarding the very costly peace keeping operations in which the United Nations is now engaged. Canadian acceptance of the court's decision was naturally forthcoming, and through our efforts in the fifth committee steps have been taken which look very hopeful in respect to establishing a sound basis for the financial
Supply-External Affairs operations of the United Nations. In connection therewith there comes into our minds what looks to be the happy solution of the vexatious Congo problem.
The United Nations general assembly has seven committees operating for a period of three months and so, Mr. Chairman, it would be quite a simple thing for one to carry on for a long time discussing briefly but a very few of these important avenues of goodwill and important overtures to a better and more peaceful world. In the assembly the Canadian delegation made strong reference to a subject which has been mentioned by the hon. member for Essex East, the question of Soviet colonialism.
It is recalled that a strong statement, which drew tremendous attention not only in Canada but elsewhere, was made by the Prime Minister in September 1960, and I would point out it was made in the presence of Mr. Khrushchev himself. Since that time the present government has dealt with that very important problem with consistency and persistency and has spoken out very strongly on a subject which should have been spoken on with greater strength long, long ago. It is just a little bit difficult to take when one hears the Soviet union constantly denounce the United Kingdom and France on their colonial records; but last year, before the general assembly, Canada suggested that the light of public opinion be thrown on the dark areas of tyranny within the Soviet union. That was a strong statement of which Canadians may be very proud. I do not know whether or not the hon. member for Essex East will be pleased to hear this-I am sure he will, really-but I happened to be the spokesman for the government on that occasion and the number of Canadians from all over this country who praised the speech and who reiterated the approval they had given the Prime Minister in opening the subject so strongly in 1960 brought joy to my heart.
He didn't open it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I may say to the hon. lady that 'I have examined very carefully the records of the United Nations, I have read the documents probably as carefully as she has, and I say that the strongest statement ever made on this subject was made by the Prime Minister of Canada in September, 1960.

Mr. Chairman, may I inquire of the hon. member whether he will admit that what the hon. member for Essex East has said is perfectly correct; that what in fact the present Leader of the Opposition,, then the secretary of state for external affairs,, said on that and previous occasions was in,

Supply-External Affairs the same vein as the speech made by the Prime Minister, that much noted speech, and in fact what the Prime Minister said was only following along with what the Leader of the Opposition had previously said, although perhaps the hon. member may believe, because of his personal bias, that it was better said by the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I may say, Mr. Chairman, that I have listened to a great many speeches in this house and I have always been able to contain myself until they were finished before asking a question, even those delivered by the hon. lady. There is no doubt that the speeches to which she referred were in the same vein and dealt with the same subject. But perhaps she should read the whole speech. I say that this subject was opened up by the Prime Minister and that a persistently strong stand has been followed. If she wants to read the international comment on this, I invite her to do so. I very much deplore an interjection of partisanship into a discussion of foreign affairs. I would say, if I could presume to advise a man much older and more experienced than myself, that if the hon. member for Essex East is desirous of scoring a point against the Prime Minister of Canada- and no doubt he is-then he is not on very good ground, even in political terms, in dealing with this particular question, because the Prime Minister has been noted for his stalwart and outstanding championing of the *very subject matter with which we are dealing, and I do not think any charge of insin-*cerity would stick very well.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think we should look upon this whole subject as one in which -Canadians might find cause for common action and common appraisal, rather than seeking to find avenues for disagreement and the scoring of political advantage. I am not one who would ever suggest that the discharge of -Canadian foreign policy did not bring distinction to Canada in the days before the present government took office. Naturally I would not say such a thing if I did not think such a thing. I will say this, that it ill-behooves any [DOT]Canadian to draw comfort from the suggestion that our country's prestige today is not *shining and bright, because that is exactly the situation in which it stands. I have had an opportunity to see Canada in international scenes and I have heard this tribute from all sides. As a Canadian I take great pride in that fact.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask a *question of the hon. member who has just resumed his seat? Could the hon. member tell us why he has declined in his speech, which I take it was made as a spokesman on behalf of the government, to discuss the most
vital issue that now faces this parliament; that is, whether Canada should acquire nuclear weapons, and the government's stand on that issue.
Make your speech when the time comes.
No answer.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:

(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. Would the house consent to General Norstad sitting beside the Leader of the Opposition while the latter delivers his speech?
(Text):

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, that intervention represents the level of intelligence of the hon. gentleman. With regard to General Norstad, I may say that I would rather have General Norstad, a NATO commander and therefore a servant of Canada, sitting beside me than Mr. Hitler or any of his henchmen.
It is a minute before ten o'clock, Mr. Chairman, and I wonder whether I would be trespassing on the indulgence of the house if I asked it to be called ten o'clock?
Ten o'clock. (Translation):

Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I inquire from the house leader what the business will be for Monday and next week, as it was promised by the acting house leader last evening?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The business for tomorrow will be a continuation of the discussion on the estimates of the Department of External Affairs. I will announce tomorrow the business for Monday.
Give us a little bit of a break.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I am giving the Liberal party and the New Democratic party time to think over how they propose dealing with the estimates.
Order.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: You had better do a little thinking yourself. You may have to do a good deal of squirming.

speechtext: At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
